items.body: The British wagering sector has undergone significant changes in the past few years, with stricter regulations and improved safeguarding measures transforming the way punters interact with online betting sites. While these changes aim to establish a more secure environment, an growing proportion of UK bettors are seeking options beyond their domestic market, attracted by varying odds offerings, bonus structures, and wagering opportunities that may not be available domestically. The Evolving Landscape of Digital Wagering in Britain The UK gambling market has experienced significant transformation since the implementation of the Gambling Act 2005, with governing authorities implementing progressively stricter controls over advertising practices, betting limits, and player protection initiatives. The UK Gambling Commission now enforces strict affordability checks, mandatory deposit limits, and enhanced verification processes that have fundamentally altered the wagering environment for British bettors seeking adaptability in their wagering activities. Recent legislative changes, including the ban on credit card gambling and limitations on VIP schemes, have prompted many experienced bettors to reassess their choices and explore international platforms offering different regulatory frameworks. These offshore operators often offer more generous welcome bonuses, higher betting limits, and fewer restrictions on bonus promotions, creating an attractive option for those who find local laws too limiting or intrusive. The move to offshore betting platforms reflects a wider movement among UK bettors who prioritize individual autonomy, better odds, and diverse betting markets over the strictly controlled domestic environment. While licensed operators highlight customer safeguarding and gambling responsibility, many punters feel confident managing their own risk and prefer platforms that offer enhanced flexibility, improved value propositions, and a broader selection of betting opportunities without extensive monitoring. Key Advantages That Attract UK Players to Offshore Platforms The migration of British bettors towards offshore betting sites stems from various important factors that directly impact their wagering activities and potential returns. These external betting platforms often offer offerings and perks that have become increasingly restricted or unavailable within the UK market, creating a notable draw for seasoned punters looking for improved returns and versatility in their betting activities. Understanding these advantages helps explain why many experienced punters are keen to explore beyond familiar domestic brands. From monetary rewards to operational freedoms, international platforms have carved out a distinctive position by offering what many British bettors regard as superior terms and conditions for their betting activities. Enhanced Odds and Increased Betting Limits One of the primary advantages of overseas operators is their attractive price offerings, with many international operators frequently delivering superior pricing across various sports markets compared to their UK counterparts. This variance, though sometimes slight, builds considerably over time for regular bettors, potentially adding thousands of pounds to yearly profits for those regularly betting on football, horse racing, and other popular events. Additionally, offshore betting operators typically impose fewer restrictions on maximum stake sizes and potential winnings, enabling skilled bettors to bet larger amounts without facing immediate account limitations. UK-licensed operators have become increasingly quick to restrict or close accounts of profitable players, whereas many offshore platforms maintain a more tolerant approach towards skilled bettors who regularly produce winnings. Enhanced Bonus Structures and Promotions International betting platforms frequently provide substantially more appealing sign-up bonuses and regular promotional offers than those available through UK-licensed sites, which are subject to strict advertising and bonus regulations. These international betting sites can offer deposit matches of 100% or greater, complimentary bets with more favourable terms, and loyalty schemes that provide authentic long-term value to active bettors without the restrictive wagering requirements prevalent in the UK market. The promotional environment beyond UK regulatory reach allows for innovative reward frameworks such as cashback schemes, boosted parlay rewards, and loyalty tiers with tangible benefits that go further than superficial offers. For bettors capable of maximizing these promotions strategically, the extra benefits can represent a significant enhancement to their overall betting bankroll and provide opportunities simply not matched by domestic alternatives. Enhanced Freedom Beyond GAMSTOP Restrictions The GAMSTOP self-exclusion program, whilst providing a crucial protective function for problem gamblers, has generated discontent among responsible bettors who feel unjustly limited by its one-size-fits-all policy. Overseas operators operating outside UK jurisdiction are unlinked to this system, enabling bettors who have previously self-excluded—perhaps throughout a brief period of caution—to return to wagering action without waiting for lengthy exclusion periods to conclude. This freedom appeals especially to experienced punters who sustain responsible betting practices but may have registered with GAMSTOP during a challenging time or simply wish to retain full authority over their own wagering choices. Offshore platforms provide these individuals with entry to wagering opportunities without the permanent digital footprint that GAMSTOP registration creates, though this naturally requires personal responsibility and genuine evaluation regarding one’s relationship with gambling. Understanding the Regulatory Distinctions and Their Implications The UK Gambling Commission functions within among the most stringent compliance standards in the world, implementing comprehensive measures that encompass mandatory affordability checks, stake limits, and robust player protection frameworks. These regulations, while designed to protect consumers, have fundamentally altered the betting experience for many punters who find themselves subject to increased scrutiny and limitations that can constrain their betting options and general satisfaction of the pursuit. Offshore betting platforms generally function under distinct regulatory jurisdictions such as Curacao, Malta, or Gibraltar, which maintain their own compliance frameworks that often differ significantly from British requirements. These alternative jurisdictions typically enforce fewer limitations on promotional offers, allow increased betting limits, and implement more streamlined verification processes, creating an environment that many seasoned punters find more conducive to their favored approach of betting without ongoing oversight. The real-world effects of these regulatory differences go far past simple convenience, affecting everything from the speed of withdrawals to the types of promotional offers offered to customers. British-licensed operators must adhere to strict advertising standards, bonus wagering requirements, and mandatory cooling-off periods, whereas international operators can often provide more generous welcome bonuses, continuous promotional offers, and quicker withdrawal processing that appeal to punters seeking better value. Understanding these jurisdictional differences helps explain why some bettors actively seek alternatives to domestic platforms, particularly those who feel over-regulated or believe their betting activities are being unnecessarily monitored. While UK regulations prioritize player protection and responsible gambling, the trade-off involves reduced flexibility and autonomy that certain punters find overly restrictive, leading them to explore options where they can enjoy a more traditional betting experience with fewer administrative hurdles and greater personal control over their gambling decisions. Popular Characteristics Seen on International Sports Betting Sites The appeal of offshore betting platforms extends beyond simple regulatory differences, incorporating a broad spectrum of features that differentiate them from their UK-regulated counterparts and appeal to British bettors seeking improved wagering opportunities. These platforms typically complete crypto withdrawals within hours rather than days, removing traditional banking delays while providing punters greater control over their funds privacy and lower transaction fees. Broader Selection of Sports and Wagering Options International betting sites often grant access to specialized sporting events and international competitions that receive limited coverage on licensed UK operators, including Asian handicap markets and comprehensive esports wagering choices. The wider variety includes proposition bets, political markets, and entertainment wagering opportunities that may face restrictions under UK licensing requirements, giving punters access to thousands of extra markets. What British Punters Should Consider Before Making the Switch Before moving to international betting platforms, British bettors must thoroughly assess the legal safeguards they’ll be forgoing. UK-licensed operators provide access to the Gambling Commission’s complaint handling services, self-exclusion schemes like GAMSTOP, and guaranteed fund segregation that safeguards funds if a operator becomes insolvent. Offshore sites may offer few options if disputes arise, and punters should closely examine each platform’s licensing jurisdiction, dispute resolution procedures, and fiscal security before depositing money to ensure they’re not exposing themselves to unnecessary risks. Payment processing represents another critical consideration when assessing international betting options. UK bettors accustomed to quick payouts and familiar payment methods may face extended wait periods, foreign exchange charges, and restricted payment methods with international platforms. Some platforms refuse UK credit cards due to compliance requirements, necessitating other payment solutions like electronic payment systems, cryptocurrencies, or prepaid vouchers. Understanding the total expenses of transactions, factoring in any hidden charges or unfavourable exchange rates, helps punters assess their spending carefully and prevent surprise charges that could diminish their betting profitability. Responsible gambling tools and customer support quality should factor heavily into any choice to change platforms. While UK operators must provide comprehensive responsible gambling features including deposit limits, reality tests, and time-outs, offshore sites vary considerably in their dedication to player protection. British bettors should verify that their chosen platform offers strong protections, offers assistance in English during accessible times, and demonstrates a genuine commitment to responsible gambling practices. Checking unbiased reviews, checking licensing authority requirements, and evaluating support responsiveness before depositing significant funds can help find reliable platforms that prioritise player welfare alongside attractive promotions.

items.body: “Seu corpo que disfarça a tatuagem do desejo”: a body hiding the tattoo of desire. That is where “A Cor do que Eu Quero” opens, two people at close range, concealing things from each other anyway. Roberta Campos wrote it and sings it with Mari Froes, and it anchors Coisas de Viver a Dois, out 29 May 2026 on Sonora Digital: her album Coisas de Viver re-recorded as duets, one guest per song, with the band that toured it for a year. Campos comes from Caetanópolis, a small town in Minas Gerais, and has written for Brazilian radio and telenovelas for nearly two decades. Froes is younger, from Anápolis in Goiás; her version of “Vaitimbora” went round the world last year. They swap verses over Campos’s nylon-string guitar, Amanda Barbosa‘s drums kept low and close, Diogo Ville laying a wash of keys underneath, Jackson Lourenço and João Elbert filling in the edges on bass and electric guitar. When the chorus arrives they sing it together, close enough that the harmony feels like conversation. The song is about living with someone. Not the honeymoon part, the everyday part: desire, arguments, the way one sentence can change the mood of a whole house. Campos gets it into three words: “Palavras mudando tudo”, words changing everything. Listen to “A Cor do que Eu Quero” and stream Coisas de Viver a Dois HERE The post Daily Discovery: Roberta Campos x Mari Froes – A Cor do que Eu Quero appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Discipleship, as practised at Terry Riley’s Kirana East, turns the Western paradigm of individual creativity on its head, argues Ryan Meehan The train had taken me some three hours out of Tokyo to Kobuchizawa, a hamlet in Japan’s Southern Alps – a first taste of countryside quiet beyond the reach of the megacities. My contact meets me at the station: Hiromitsu Hirata, who will serve as my translator for the day, having learned English during his time studying music and philosophy in India. He’s also the newest of Terry Riley’s disciples at Kirana East, the small but vibrant raga school founded by Riley after he relocated to Japan in 2020. Another student and I climb into Hiro’s silver van to reach a house beside a meadow. Through a doorway on the garden deck, we enter a sunlit living room brimming with musical instruments and speaker equipment, where a handful of students are already seated around our instructor Sara Miyamoto. It’s only by chance that I’m able to sit in for this introductory class. Now 91, Riley no longer gives interviews; the lessons he teaches are private, and only for the advanced. But as luck would have it, this basic class falls within the window of my visit to Japan, and Miyamoto has given her blessing to join the circle as an observer. With conversation buzzing around me, I shuffle through a packet of instruction materials written by Riley. I first became acquainted with kirana gharana (a signature music style of northern India) while covering a birthday celebration event held by La Monte Young for the late kirana singer Pandit Pran Nath (see The Wire 443), the guru shared by Young and Riley until Nath’s death in 1996. I’ve sought out Kirana East with a degree of confidence in my understanding of its basic premises. Almost immediately, however, the complications of even this short introduction begin to envelop me in dread. There is the sargam, the Indian equivalent of solfeggio, with its specific proportion of sharps and flats; the gamaks, technical flourishes with which the singer moves between the notes; the all-important alap, the raga’s slow introductory motif, which we will be practising as a group. I am not a student of any substance in this music, I say to myself; I’m not even a musician. My trip here has been an imposition, a gesture of real arrogance. In deepening embarrassment, my eyes scan across the page to a phrase underlined in bold: “In practice, you don’t have to be too concerned with this.” Its placement seems like a pin to pop my ballooning panic, and with my relief comes a convulsion of laughter. When I explain, Miyamoto smiles: “That’s so Terry.” Without much ceremony, the lesson gets underway. Miyamoto guides the group through a series of preparatory exercises. Eyes closed, the mind acclimates to stillness, and with each new prompt – about body and mind; awareness of sound, consciousness, and position within the universe – the suggestion that music might be a parallel domain, a constitutive fabric of reality, begins to seem plausible. Miyamoto’s prompts (as translated into my ear by Hiro) are not unlike those of an especially attuned yoga class, only instead of the repetitions of bodily poses, we begin cycling through clusters of notes at the foundations of kirana singing. Her voice is crystalline, gliding between pitches with precision, polishing the rough edges I hear in my own. A lesson like this requires a curious mixture of discipline and relaxation: one maintains concentration and control over one’s own tone, while at the same time giving oneself over to the larger sonority of the group. It’s challenging and meditative and pleasurable, and before I can get my hands around it, it’s over. Miyamoto first heard raga via an Ali Akbar Khan album in the record collection of her family, whose Japanese musical underground ties are extensive. The studio where she teaches, Hoshi To Niji (Star And Rainbow), was founded by her father in the back of his dental practice, and has hosted decades’ worth of recordings, the most recent among which are some by Eiko Ishibashi and Jim O’Rourke, as well as her own collaborations with Riley. She began her life as a musician playing bass, and first met Riley during his 2017 trip to Japan for an event programmed by her husband. “When I saw Terry’s concert in Japan, I was so shocked how much information the sound included. Just a single note he played from the melodica brought tears to my eyes.” She leapt at the opportunity to take instruction from him. “At the time I didn’t have any idea what ‘disciple’ meant. I was not planning to study raga. I just wanted to keep my life going as a musician.” There’s something poetic about the hazard with which Miyamoto found herself embarking on gurukula, the master-disciple relationship that helps to maintain the classical raga tradition. As disciples of Pran Nath, Young and his wife Marian Zazeela were not above tying his shoes if it meant making his life “more beautiful”. While the demands of discipleship are unique in each case, the underlying devotion is absolute. It amounts to a sacrifice of a notion of personal freedom in exchange for total access to the wisdom and guidance of a venerated elder. “Being a disciple means totally losing my ego,” explains Miyamoto. “I am not the first priority in my life at the moment, and I have to be open for every study from Terry. The outline of myself has totally vanished, and I don’t have to think about that.” The intensity of the gurukula relationship can be unnerving to those on the outside of it. In the Western mainstream, musicians are stars; we glorify the autodidacts, the iconoclasts, the rootless young. By contrast, the late composer Michael Harrison sat beside La Monte Young for nearly a decade, adjusting his guru’s tuning for the performance of The Well-Tuned Piano, a piece Harrison was only allowed to perform once on his own, and then only in private. Young’s closest disciple Jung Hee Choi has described gurukula as “the most demanding long-term art project”. For Hiro, this contrast is a matter of perspective: “We are always educated in modern society as an individual who has the right to choose. We are supposed to have judgement and reasoning. In general, in the Eastern tradition, education is the opposite. When we start, we are blind. We don’t have the ability to choose the path we go. That’s why we need a guru, the one who removes the darkness and shows the path. Because we are not yet able to judge, we should surrender to someone we think trustworthy.” If discipleship remains niche as a way of life, other aspects of kirana hold unmistakable appeal in the Western avant garde, with figures such as Jon Hassell, Don Cherry and Catherine Hennix all taking instruction from Pran Nath during his lifetime. Perhaps this influence is preparing the ground, in some form or another, for its resurgence. This essay appears in The Wire 510. Wire subscribers can also read it in our online magazine library.

items.body: Review by toroddreincarnated — Beware, this is probably my one and only review here as I run my own blog. This box deserves moreattention than my review blog can give it. Hence this review...The 8 studio albums plus 1 live album plus a couple of leftover songs from this band.All the albums were released as CD-R in 100 copies each. They were also released locally in the Bodoarea (where they were based) and are almost impossible to find. Hence this box. Hence this review.The man behind the band was Odd Fredrik Fezza Ellingsen, ex Host, Akasha and St. Helena. He was themain force on one of Scandinavia's early masterpieces of progressive rock; Host's Hardt Mot Hardtalbum (1976).In my reviews of Lovetann's eight albums for my own blog, I have compared them to Thule's Natt opus.I have also, tongue in cheek, labelled Lovetann and Thule as Arctic Prog bands. There is some truthin this label, but this suggestion is only half-serious.Lovetann's music is a unique blend of folk-rock and art-rock. The vocals are baryton operaticvocals. This band was one of the truly originals in the progressive rock scene. Their location wellbeyond the Arctic Circle and 1000 miles/1500 km from the nearest progressive rock scene (Trondheim/Oslo) also gave the band its own sound and style.I have below copied over extracts of the reviews of the eight albums previously reviewed & publishedin my own blog The Sound Of Fighting Cats. This is the only way to review this box in the fairestway.I Lovens Hule 1999The debut album. The music is a blend of prog folk and heavy prog. Both Thule and Host are good references. There arealso some Jethro Tull references here. I am tempted to label the music here and indeed Thule's music as Arctic Prog. The music and soundare pretty unique. That's not least because of the pretty operatic male vocals. The music is alsobombastic and slightly symphonic. The songs are pretty long with a lot of progressions throughout the songs. The vocals are good, butthe star here is the very good guitar solos and riffs.That makes this a good album indeed and one to check out. This album is indeed a hidden gem and oneto check out.En Dag Som Love 1999 The music is a blend of dark art-rock and dark symphonic prog. Both Thule and Host are goodreferences.As I did in the review of their debut album, I am tempted to label their music as Arctic Prog. Thisas they have the same depressive, dark sound and take on progressive rock and art-rock as theirbrethren 1000 km further north, Thule. Both Lovetann and Thule released their music well north ofthe Arctic Circle.The music is made even darker by some dark operatic male vocals, darkened guitar harmonies andguitar solos. The bass is also brooding.The four songs are all good and this is another good album from this band. This is an album fans of Thule and dark prog should check out.Ansikt Til Ansikt 2000 The music is again pretty special. The music is a blend of dark art-rock and dark symphonic prog.Thule is again a good reference. There are some more dark psych rock this time around. Arctic Prog is what I would label their and Thule music as I did in my reviews of their first twoalbums. That does not really give any meaning.. The vocals are again dark operatic male vocals.This album is not as good as their first two albums. This is still a pretty good album.. but still abit of a disappointment. Sfinks 2000The music is again what I would define as arctic prog. The band is from beyond the Arctic Circlewith total darkness for 5 months of the year. The same goes for Thule, another band in this region,although 1000 km further north. That means a blend of dark folk rock and art-rock. There are also some hints of symphonic prog here.The music is depressive with some guitar solos and operatic baritone Norwegian vocals on top of thesound.The music is muscular but not particularly heavy. There are some good Jethro Tull influencesthroughout this album. This is not their finest album. The quality is pretty good though. Fans of Scandinavian prog rockshould check out this album.Oye For Oye 2001 The music is again a blend of dark folk rock and art-rock. There are also some hints of symphonicprog here. The music is mid-tempo and dark. The guitars from Odd Fezza Ellingsen (Host etc etc) are the dominant instrument here. The dark operatic male vocals also give this album a lot of character. The sound is good and there is a lot of Arctic ambience here. Those who love Thule will also findthis album enjoyable and interesting.The quality here is pretty good. I am not won over by this album. It is still an interesting albumand an original take on progressive rock, art-rock and folk rock.Lovehjerte 2001 The music is an eclectic blend of folk rock, art-rock and early symphonic prog. Both Host and Thule are good references here. The music is a bit vaudeville and operatic at times. That is not at least because of the vocals. Themain vocals are operatic male vocals. The lyrics are a mix of Norwegian and English. The band has moved in a more vaudeville art-rock direction on the last couple of albums. This albumis very much in that direction. The sound is good. The music also sounds like it is influenced by the dark nights beyond the Arctic Circle where thisband comes from. The quality of the music is pretty good and this makes it an interesting album. It is an album forthose who are looking for something original and special. Something unique and exotic.Fugl Foniks 2003 The music is a blend of folk rock, art-rock and heavy prog. There are also some symphonic proginfluences here.This type of prog, both this band and Thule 1000 km further north in Norway were doing, deserves itsown label... Arctic Prog. The reason is that the music is pretty unique and very much rooted in thelife and landscape beyond the Arctic Circle.The lyrics are now entirely in English this time around and a departure from the Norwegian lyrics ontheir first albums. The music is pretty hard with some raw guitars. The vocals are both operatic and good. The music is pretty good. This is not one of their best albums. Nevertheless, this is an album wellworth checking out.The Times 2013The music is again a blend of folk-rock and art-rock. There are also a lot of eclectic prog here.Their albums have become more and more eclectic on each album. This album is pretty close to beingan eclectic prog album. I would still label their music as Arctic Prog.There are some very good guitars here. Mostly guitar solos and harmonies. The operatic vocals are also very good here. These vocals is giving Lovetann's music it's ownidentity.The vocals are entirely in English and this makes this album more accessible for the Englishspeaking prog rock fans.The quality is good throughout and this album offers some good value for money. This is perhapstheir best album ever.That is these 8 albums. There is also a good live album in the box too.This box has been released in a limited number. This box is something unique in the progressive rockscene and can only be purchased from Norske Albumklassikere directly. Collectors of Scandinavian progressive rock, rare progressive rock and other collectors shouldpurchase this box. For these reasons, all three of them, that is I purchased this box. I was notdisappointed with it as the music and the packaging are great.The album can be purchased directly from Norske Albumklassikere at their webshop

items.body: Review by Nickmannion — In 1975 when cash is short but your burgeoning music passion is growing exponentially the then mail order record clubs "5 albums for �1" were one way to grow your collection. Yes this was one of my joining offers 5! And I still have the self same copy. I knew who Ginger Baker was, the Gurvitz brothers not so much, but backloading my knowledge, they came from Three Man Army (whose albums I now have) and this is BGA's debut album.I actually really rate this album and is the best of their three studio efforts although the retro released 'Live in Derby '75' is my favourite and well worth finding the cd.So, what we don't have is drum dominated Cream/Airforce-esque re-treads but a very much of its time 'serious' rock music. For those not there, there was no in between, it was either pop for the masses (mostly an utter utter waste of time) or 'progressive' (what today we would term as 'metal' back then was always considered progressive ie Sabbath and so forth). This album, maybe due to familiarity, conjures up 1975 from the first groove to the last fade which is just a bit marvellous. So we get, if not a mish mash, then different approaches to the then rock oeuvre, from the sophisticated blues of '4 Phil' (great guitarist Mr Gurvitz) to the extended 'rock opera' of 'Mad Jack' (not sure but there was a film called Death Race 2000 that came out about this time and the 'tale' of Mad Jack sums it up). Actually the other comparisons to this track are two SAHB songs..'The Tale of the Giant Stone Eater' and ' Hot City Symphony/Vambo'....and both bands were managed by Bill Fehilly so maybe there was some cross fertilisation with this template. Every days a school day huh? 'Memory Lane' gives Baker his spotlight...am no drummer but wow...'Help Me' the opener really rocks out but has the most proggy keys layers too. 'Love Is' does the one thing I can't abide...orchestration behind/as part of a rock/prog song...and the jagged Hendrix type blues rock of the riff does not need any enhancement ..ok?! 'Inside Of Me' is the track that grabs. A simple repeated guitar refrain over descending minor key backing is so so so 1975 and so so perfect. I Wanna Live Again is orchestrated newly divorced self pitying angst and the one that could be cut. 'Since Beginning' could turn up on a Gentle Giant album...yes really...minus any baroque GG leanings ...and is the most 'ambitious' track. I know we shouldn't be influenced by the time/place/memories this conjures up...I can even picture my favourite tea mug I used to hug and drink from when you sat and listened...and believe it or not young uns, did nothing else but listen ...to albums as we did way back when...and the inner double page 'poster' that used to be in Sounds magazine of Paul Kossoff that was above my stereo on the wall ...but am going to give this a 4 even if it is 3.6ish. Try the above mentioned live CD...they had a full time keyboard player and singer by then and I saw them on that tour...which is a better representation of the band.

items.body: Review by Nickmannion — In one of those 'coincidences' that life throws up, I went to the same school as Norm Barratt but was 9 or 10 years younger (and am not sure about Gravy Train forming in Manchester as he lived nearer Liverpool but I digress...) and in the summer term of '74 school, who had quite a big hall and stage at one end, gave out free tickets for 'a concert' where a group including an ex pupil (yup..) were going to film themselves playing to us the audience, for promo purposes and now , I also assume, for this album in particular*. Long story short, the electrics couldn't cope with the back line/PA/lights and film gear and they blew. The band ended up miming to probably this album and the whole thing fell a bit flat. I can't even get to say I saw them 'live' although at the time I had no idea who they were and if it wasn't Sabbath or Purple I can't say I would have been impressed either...well, you know, we have all been 14/15...Yes I now know full well who they are/were and am reviewing this album first (I have them all) due to the above. I have got a cd copy as my vinyl was a bit battered and never found one priced 'at my worth' to upgrade, hence the cd replaced it. It does have 'bonus tracks' which I will dismiss here as utterly dire, from when NB went all Xian 'rock' and never get played.OK the album itself. Hmmmm. My least favourite of theirs and in summary a cross between BJH and Fruupp fronted by Demis Roussos...unfortunately in his Euro pop cross over period and not his time in Aphrodites Child...and BJH and Fruupp not on a good day either. I may be misremembering but I think the film above was for the American market as the flyers/tickets stated and maybe this is why this album is less than inspiring and what you might called 'watered down'. The title track is the best example and has a fair few prog influences that are sort of skirted with (other than the two I have mentioned)...maybe Greenslade and Supertramp being others... but it doesn't get out of 1st gear and the vocals (see comparison above) are over wrought and could have been fronting a non British '74 Eurovision entry. And comparing it to their wilder Tull twisted heavy blues drenched first effort say, it just leaves me non plussed. It certainly 'ain't heavy' and maybe an already out of their time band having one last throw of the dice at 'success' hence the compromises. Sorry Norm but even though we share an alma mater, I can't rate this album too high and it has not aged well. Yes I would probably go 2.75 but it isn't 'good' so I cannot give it a 3. * I have scoured the net and found no footage anywhere so it probably got binned or, with the electrics issue, they may not have got anything on celluloid either...but it did happen!

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — The Wow! Signal is mostly a very good album, with only a couple of songs that I feel are weaker than the rest.[I really think that if all bands looked at their albums as a single entity, rather than just a collection of individual songs, we could avoid the "filler syndrome"?the "gee, why don't we just toss this song on there?" mentality. A record's grooves should be considered sacred, deserving only of the very best work a band can create. Every track should have a reason to exist.]That said, I can't imagine any fan being disappointed by The Wow! Signal. It's got all the signature elements I personally love about this band: Matt Bellamy's passionate vocal style, the dramatic, ever-present tech and sci-fi vibes, Chris Wolstenholme's stellar bass work?especially on "Nightshift Superstar"?and plenty of wild electric guitar. Admittedly, my exposure to the band is still somewhat limited. I own Black Holes and Revelations and have done reaction videos to a number of their songs over the years, but I certainly wouldn't call myself an expert. I also love hearing the echoes of classical composers woven into Bellamy's songwriting.Muse has always excelled at creating a larger-than-life sound, and on this album that sense of scale is amplified by sweeping orchestral arrangements on several tracks?most dramatically on the opener, "The Dark Forest," which reminded me of epic film scores like Lawrence of Arabia and other grand cinematic works of that era.They're playing to their strengths as musicians and songwriters. Even a weaker track like "The Sickness in You and I" is partially redeemed by its strong chorus. On the other hand, there's a fair bit of progressive metal chugging that I'm sure fans of the genre will enjoy, but it strikes me as just a little out of place. It feels playful, almost as if the band is having fun with the style, but at times it comes across as something added to strengthen the track rather than something the song truly needed.The very pop-oriented track "Hush" (which, unsurprisingly, is not really my thing) features guest vocalist Ellie Goulding. It's a cool addition, and the song did grow on me somewhat, but I have to ask: is this really the direction Muse wants to pursue? I hope not.Lyrically, The Wow! Signal continues Muse's fascination with big ideas: technology, humanity's place in the universe, dystopian themes, and the tension between progress and consequence.I give the album 4 out of 5 dog bones. It's a pretty cool record, with enough diversity across the songs to eliver a satisfying platter of musical fun.

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — If you haven't heard of this band out of BC, Canada, it's understandable. Independent bands often struggle to be heard above the ever-growing wave of progressive music flooding the scene. That doesn't make them any less deserving of your attention. There aren't many five-piece progressive rock bands with a female majority, which makes them stand out before you've even heard a note.One thing that didn't help, at least for me, was the band's name. Pareidolon isn't quite as easy to remember as Yes, Rush, or Opeth, and I initially had trouble recalling it. Thankfully, the music leaves a much stronger impression than the name.Listening through this expansive album is quite the revelation. After the deceptively straightforward opening track, the album takes a fearless leap into the unknown, carrying the listener along for a ride that feels like jumping from an airplane with nothing but a parachute. It's exhilarating, with moments where the sheer rush of air leaves you breathless in the best possible way, and ultimately, it's immensely rewarding.This album would likely boggle the mind of an unsuspecting non-prog listener while delighting any serious modern fan of progressive music. Be aware, though, that this is an expansive release approaching double-album length?there is simply so much compelling music here, and the album represents eight years of work. Let's start with the gorgeous artwork on the cover by Jordan Weiss. It perfectly captures the spirit of the album: vast and full of movement, with dramatic peaks and valleys that mirror the music's dynamic shifts. In fact, the artwork was chosen before the album was finished, becoming a visual touchstone that helped guide the band's creative journey toward the final result.If I were to sum up this album, the best way I can put it is: it rocks. The songs are intricate, adventurous, and uniquely structured; the musicianship is exceptional; the female vocals are both refreshing and captivating; and the band takes all the ingredients we love from classic prog and infuses them with a modern edge. You'll find flute, thunderous bass and drums, piano and synth keyboards galore, both heavy and acoustic guitar, complex instrumental interludes, and a cohesive thematic concept that binds the entire album together: the pursuit of a goal, the challenges along the way, and the possibility of falling short.Some high-profile help was brought in for the album as well: Baard Kolstad of Leprous contributes drums to the complex track "Emotional Tides."I love this album. Although not for the faint of heart, it rewards the dedicated listener willing to immerse themselves in its many layers. In short, it is a remarkable modern Canadian prog work?one that deserves to be recognized among the standout releases of the genre.4.5 out of 5 dog bones from me.

items.body: Review by Aussie-Byrd-Brother — Young modern Italian band Cellar Noise delivered an appealing debut `Alight' back in 2017, a charming first effort grounded firmly in the tradition of vintage RPI works. Their follow-up, `Nautilus', only two years later saw a complete abrupt turn, the group embracing instead a modern approach and ditching the majority of retro flavours (similar to fellow young Italian group Ingranaggi Della Valle who moved on quickly from their retro roots). Their latest, 2026's `Panic Loves Telling Lies' sees the five-piece combining both of those approaches, fusing a contemporary heaviness with extravagant classical fancy, then grafting them to sophisticated song-writing, and it results in their strongest and most polished effort yet, with a range of international influences revealing themselves throughout.The band describe their third album as being "centred around the experience of being trapped within one's own mind, held captive by rigid mental constructs shaped by fear and self-deception. Defence mechanisms created as safety nets and survival tools, both reassuring and deceptive at the same time. However, as balance slowly deteriorates and panic intensifies, a subtle possibility of freedom emerges beneath the surface: breaking free from the cage and reclaiming one's true self, allowing a moment's respite for an exhausted and overwhelmed mind." That sense of melancholy and holding back, only to be confronted with traces of hope and light emerges constantly throughout the disc.It's instantly noticeable on opener `Wasted Potential' that vocalist Francesco Lovari, singing in charmingly accented English, is sounding more confident and natural than ever, with his weary vocal drolly delivering an introspective and dour lyric ("Every success brings less conviction" sure ain't smiles and sunshine!) over a maddening electronic loop, punchy riffing and wall-to-wall icy Mellotron, a cowering prettiness trying to break through the unhappiness.There's a gutsy crunch to `Please Be Gentle', with snarling and twitchy staccato riffing around gently pleading words, and it wouldn't have sounded out of place on a Haken album.The dramatic and atmospheric twelve-minute album standout `The Case of the Silent Queen' might be one of the strongest and most lavish pieces the band has ever delivered, with ravishing instrumentation and a purposeful sense of build, with gorgeous piano and keyboards that take on an elegant orchestration-like grandness. The group here reminds of everything from early Genesis, Steven Wilson and fellow young Italian (and now sadly seemingly defunct) band Unreal City, even calling to mind `Pure/Passion'-era Pendragon with their cross of heavier guitars while still retaining the more retro-flavoured `romantic' flavours, and the brooding second half creeps with a Goblin-like erupting menace (and there's a lovely call-back to a grand theme from their debut buried in there as well as a gift to long-time fans and close listeners!).One of the loveliest pieces on the disc, `We Need to Talk' is a soft acoustic indie pop/rocker with introspective words that recalls the indie/alt pop moments of Porcupine Tree's `Stupid Dream/Lightbulb Sun' era, and restrained cello strains brings a touch of Anekdoten's soul-searching. Framed around darkly sexy grooving riffing ala tracks like Porcupine Tree's `Strip the Soul', the Riverside-esque `Caged' holds one of the biggest choruses of the disc, a richly layered vocal with a vulnerable lyric and exquisitely arranged harmonies.Like a cross between Zombi and Lunatic Soul, slinking electronics, shimmering electric piano, murmuring bass and pulsing programmed beats slink through `The Day We Never Met', ghostly Mellotron rising like a gothic choir, and the self-titled closer `Panic Loves Telling Lies' is a pensive indie rocker that embraces the heart of some of the later Anathema works, making for a humble and subdued way to finish.Perhaps many of the tracks fall back on a similar pattern - bring the heavy guitars, launch the Mellotron! - and the band wears their current influences on their sleeves, but `Panic Loves Telling Lies' still showcases Cellar Noise's strong song-writing arrangements and vibrant instrumentation, and is more naturally melodic with richer and more expansive harmonies. It's another fine effort from the talented young quintet, and the group should be very proud of their efforts here.Three and a half stars, rounded up to four for the Archives.

items.body: Review by UMUR — "Silent Fall" is the debut full-length studio album by Romanian technical/progressive metal actPsycho Symphony. The album was independently released in 1997. Psycho Symphony formed in 1992 andreleased three demos prior to recording and releasing "Silent Fall". The album was originally onlyreleased on cassette tape but saw a CD reissue in 2000. It saw a digital/second CD reissue in 2025through Loud Rage Music.Listening to "Silent Fall" you have to wonder how many other obscure but highly worthy of beinglistened to releases are out there that not enough people know about. On the other hand it wasprobably hard for a Romanian band who released their first album on cassette tape in 1997 to getmuch attention, but they really should have gotten a lot more praise in the late 1990s because"Silent Fall" is a bit of a gem in the technical/progressive metal genre. Artists like Mekong Delta,Zero Hour, Toxik, Voivod, Realm, and Sieges Even come to mind but Psycho Symphony feel like they areall over the place in terms of influences. It�s controlled chaos though and there is a compositionalred thread throughout the album. The musicianship is through he roof. Psycho Symphony are incredibly skilled musicians and althoughthe vocals are arguably the weak link of the music, they really aren�t bad. Guitarist/lead vocalistEmil Gherasim�s voice just lacks a distinct sound and therefore his performance is good but notgreat. The drums and bass are jazz/fusion influenced and busy (both bass and drums are audible inthe mix), and the two guitars play one creative riff and melody after another. While there are someregular heavy/thrash metal riffs here and there, they are few and far between. Psycho Symphonyinstead whip up a storm of unconventional songwriting ideas and riffs and "Silent Fall" is as aresult an adventurous musical journey where you�re constantly challenged. There is still power anddrive in the music though, so this is not technical noodling for the sake of it. Everything makessense within the context of the album.Considering the place of recording (a 1990s Eastern European country) and the time of release,"Silent Fall" features a powerful, heavy, clear, and detailed sound production where everyinstrument and vocal part are audible in the mix. There�s a nice organic quality to the sound and itfeels like a real band playing. Upon conclusion it�s hard not to be impressed by "Silent Fall" (andPsycho Symphony in general) which is a high quality debut release. It deserves a lot more attentionthan it has gotten so far and fans of technical/progressive metal should take notice and give it alisten. A 4 - 4.5 star (85%) rating is deserved.(Originally posted on Metal Music Archives).

items.body: Review by greenpete — This is an essential album for Ayers fans as it collects choice singles, B-sides, outtakes together in one package. Ayers' best solo work covered the Joy of a Toy through Bananamour years, so it's no surprise the best songs here are his earliest. Of particular note is the gorgeous "Gemini Child" and French-sung "Jolie Madame." Also of note are "Singing a Song in the Morning" (Syd Barrett was on guitar on a different version), "Soon, Soon, Soon," "Stars," and "Puis Je?" (a French-language "May I"). The remainder will be familiar to those who have Ayers' albums, or are the bon vivant Caribbean, uh, "ditties" that he had such an affinity for.If you're unfamiliar with Kevin Ayers, I recommend either of his albums Joy of a Toy or Whatevershebringswesing. Or the compilation released by See For Miles. Then, if you're like me, you'll be so smitten with this one-of-a-kind Canterbury Scene psych-prog tunesmith, you'll be gathering every Ayers product you can lay your hands on. I envy you your journey!

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the many modern Italian prog acts that has kept the classic 70s years alive by reviving itand making it relevant in the 21st century, the Cuneo based PANDORA emerged in 2005 as the fatherand son team of keyboardist Beppo Colombo and drummer / bassist / guitarist / flautist /keyboardist / vocalist Claudio Colombo who together set sail into the new frontiers of Italian progof the current millennium. Together with lead vocalist Corrado Grappeggia, this trio has embarked ona journey that has yielded four albums and crucial appraise. In addition to the core power trio, theband's debut release DRAMMA DI UN POETA UBRIACO (Drama Of A Drunken Poet) also featured guitaristChristian Dimasi who would soon depart after this album's release.A veritable rekindling of 70s spirit shines on this album that goes down memory lane with the RPIretro highway passing by classic greats such as PFM, Banco, Bigletto di Bronzo, Museo Rosenbach andothers but also finds new life with references to the melodic prog metal of bands like DreamTheater, neo-prog stalwarts IQ, Arena and Pendragon as well as the usual suspects of classicsymphonic prog, namely Yes and Genesis. Delivering an album of seven stealthy tracks culminatingwith the near 14-minute closing prog behemoth "Salto nel Bulo" that collectively slink past the 63-minute mark, DRAMMA DI UN POETA UBRIACO delivers everything a retro progger with a modern sheencould possibly hope for. It's as dramatic as the title suggests all the while tempering the classicmelodic sensibilities with a touch of contemporary contrast. The mix is intoxicating indeed.While the slow burn intro that features a collage of multilingual dialogue offers a rather clumsystart as the first impressions, the band quickly falls into place with the opening "Il GiudizioUniversale" quickly showcasing Claudio's percussive prowess in full form which perfectly augmentsthe classic RPI sounds to a much more magnanimous and technically infused level of competency.Likewise the strong songwriting advances new takes on classic melodic techniques that still soundexhilarating some half decade after the fact. Nice touches of heavy angular guitar riffing generatesan energetic drive that is unprecedented in the 70s even by the heavier bands such as Biglietto perl'Inferno however never reaching the true metal camp as a few acts such as early Procession or IlRevescio della Medaglia who dished out their Italian proto-metal. The beauty of this is that theintensity of the keys and subordinate instrumentation maintains a similar energetic ecstasy whichmakes this a compelling release on many levels..The album immediately picks up momentum and tracks like "March To Hell," "Cos� Come Sei" and themonstrosity "Pandora" take the band's technical wizardry and playing chops to the brink beforepulling back on the more contemplative palette cleanser "Breve Storia di San George" set to abreezier acoustic chill vibe however after an equally laid back intro, the crafty title track burstsback into the high energy stance that the band had maintained throughout the first half of the act.The album culminates with the epic sounding "Salto nel Bulo" which captures the band's most sweepingmovements from soft contemplative ballad-like motifs to the full heavy complex procedures thatelevates the band's technical abilities. Overall the album could've been edited down about 15minutes to be a cohesively satisfying journey where then meets now but as it is it's certainly aworthy modern day excursion into the world of 21st RPI that maintains good relations with theancestors.

items.body: Beethoven completed his Piano Sonata No. 14 in 1801 and published it the following year, one of a pair issued under the heading quasi una fantasia, meaning in the manner of a fantasy. He dedicated it to a young pupil, the Countess Giulietta Guicciardi. The famous “Moonlight” name was not the composer’s own. It came from a later writer, the poet Ludwig Rellstab, whose image of moonlight on a still lake gave the piece its lasting nickname. The name stuck so firmly that the sonata is now among the most played of all piano works, known less for the storm of its finale than for the stillness of its opening. The sonata breaks with convention by placing its weight at the end rather than the start. It opens not with a bright sonata-allegro but with a slow, veiled Adagio, its steady triplets and muted sonority holding to a single subdued mood. A short, graceful Allegretto follows, a brief lightening between the darkness on either side. Then comes the Presto agitato, a stormy finale in full sonata form that carries the real drama of the piece and makes the greatest demands on the player. Beethoven asked that the whole first movement be played with the sustaining pedal held down, so the harmonies blur into a soft, resonant halo that pianists still balance in different ways. Some lean into Romantic atmosphere and rubato, others into classical clarity of line, and a few turn to the lighter fortepiano of Beethoven’s own day. That is where these recordings part company. Here are The Classic Review editorial team’s recommendations for the best recordings of Beethoven’s Piano Sonata No. 14 (“Moonlight”). Murray Perahia Perahia’s is among the most carefully considered accounts on the list, prepared from his own close study of the score. He opens the first movement softly and without hurry, holding a steady pulse that neither drags nor presses, and he runs the three movements together as a single arc. The gentle Allegretto arrives like light breaking after the shadowed opening. His finale is fluent and cleanly fingered, though it stays a shade more contained than the stormiest versions here. This is a refined, unforced Moonlight for listeners who prize clarity over drama. Read the full review of this album here Perahia Amazon Presto Apple Emil Gilels Gilels brings a serene composure to the Moonlight that sets it slightly apart from the more volatile readings here. His first movement is quiet and beautifully weighted, the triplets kept level and the tone never pressed, so the music settles into something close to a slow hymn. He carries that same control into the finale, shaping its agitation with a firm hand rather than letting it run wild. Few pianists match the evenness of his touch or the depth of his sound. Gilels Amazon Presto Apple Arthur Rubinstein Rubinstein came to this sonata late and recorded it in his mid-seventies, and the playing has the ease of a man with nothing left to prove. He keeps the opening plain, with only the slightest give in the pulse, so the line stays grave rather than sentimental. He gives unusual care to the little middle movement, which many pianists treat as a throwaway between the outer two. The finale is steady and clear without being driven hard. This is the Moonlight of a grand lyric style, warmer and less austere than Brendel. Rubinstein Amazon Presto Apple András Schiff Recorded live, Schiff’s account puts the score itself first. His first movement flows more freely than most, taken at a gentle two beats to the bar so it moves forward. He follows Beethoven’s own veiling of the sound closely, blending the harmonies under a sustained pedal. When the finale arrives he meets its drama head on, and the concert setting lends the outburst an extra charge. It thinks harder about the letter of the score than almost any reading here, yet still remains highly controversial. Schiff Amazon Presto Apple Maria João Pires This is the first of Pires’s two recordings of the sonata, and the more direct of the pair. Where her later remake grew slower and more inward, here she is quicker and plainer-spoken, letting the first movement move without lingering over its atmosphere. The reading has a clean, unfussy line and a bright clarity well suited to the music’s fantasy marking. Her finale is fleet and lightly sprung rather than heavy. It offers a fresher, more classical view than the weightier readings around it, and it wears that directness well. Pires Amazon Presto Apple Paul Lewis Lewis takes a cool, refined view, smoothing away the roughness that some pianists press into the music. His tone is beautifully graded and his fingerwork suave, and he shapes the sonata more through color and texture than through changes of speed. The playing is at its most personal in the little Allegretto, which he draws out with slight lingerings and soft swells of dynamic. Few here are as polished or as finely finished. Lewis Amazon Presto Apple Ronald Brautigam Brautigam plays a fortepiano of Beethoven’s own day, and it changes the whole character of the piece. The lighter action and bell-like upper register clear away the thick Romantic haze, so the first movement sounds spare and eerie rather than merely dreamy. Freed of that weight, his tempos are brisk and his manner refreshingly free of sentiment. The real payoff is the finale, which fairly crackles, every note of the fast figuration clear and biting in a way a modern grand can blur. For anyone curious how this music sounded on the pianos of Beethoven’s time, it is the essential choice. Brautigam Amazon Presto Apple Alfred Brendel Brendel recorded the Moonlight three times, and this is the second, from the 1970s. It is a reserved, patient reading, closer in spirit to the classical poise than to overt Romantic feeling. Everything is weighed and clearly voiced, the structure always audible beneath the surface. Set beside the warmer readings here it can seem sober, and it gives up its rewards slowly. This is a thinking musician’s Moonlight, one of the most searching first movements on the list. Brendel Amazon Presto Apple Maurizio Pollini Pollini approaches the Moonlight with an analyst’s clarity, every strand of the texture cleanly separated. He uses notably little pedal in the first movement, so the harmonies never cloud over, yet the line stays relaxed and singing rather than cold. It is in the finale that his command really tells. The rushing arpeggios come through with a hard, glinting brightness, each one struck distinct, over a left hand that holds the music to an unusually firm tread. Warmth and mystery are not really his aim here. For control and transparency, though, few on the list rival him. Pollini Amazon Presto Apple Stephen Kovacevich Kovacevich draws the sharpest contrast here between the sonata’s two extremes. His first movement is among the most tender on record, the murmuring triplets kept soft and even, its small climaxes swelling and receding without ever breaking the calm. Then he throws himself into the finale, one of the most violent ever set down. The racing arpeggios stay crisp and distinct, and the great hammered chords hit hard without turning to mere noise. Nothing spills into chaos, though. It is a thrilling, tightly held reading. Kovacevich Amazon Presto Apple Bonus Choice: Benno Moiseiwitsch Moiseiwitsch belonged to the grand Romantic school of pianism, and this 1941 recording sounds like it. He plays with a freedom that few would risk today, bending the pulse and voicing the melody with a singer’s instinct. The famous opening is unhurried and finely colored, its rubato applied with a light hand rather than pulled about. The sound is plainly of its era, but the poetry comes through undimmed. It stands here as a reminder of an older, more personal way of playing Beethoven that the later readings, for all their polish, do not attempt. items.body: Castle Party 2026 ran from 16 to 19 July at Bolków Castle in Poland. Side-Line freelancer Karo Kratochwil attended all four days of the festival, from the Thursday opening on the Park Stage to the Sunday closing sets on the Castle Stage. This report covers her route through the weekend, band by band. This year I did something I had slowly stopped believing I would do again: I took on all four days of Castle Party. For several years, my festival visits had become more selective. I would arrive later, leave earlier, choose the concerts that mattered most and protect whatever energy remained for photography, writing and the unavoidable logistics of moving through Bolków with far too much equipment. This time, I decided to give the festival the full stretch from Thursday to Sunday. Four days sound manageable when reduced to a programme. In reality, they mean repeated climbs towards the castle, fast decisions between two stages, batteries, lenses, weather forecasts, missed meals, conversations that begin unexpectedly and continue much longer than planned, clothes that never quite dry, and the growing suspicion that the person who packed the suitcase several days earlier was operating under deeply questionable assumptions. They also allow Castle Party to become a temporary reality rather than a sequence of concerts. By the final day, the town, the stages, the people and the music had begun to overlap in a way that could never be reconstructed from the running order alone. My route through Castle Party 2026 was inevitably personal. I did not see everything and would never pretend otherwise. I followed the bands that mattered to me, ran between stages when the programme became impossible, missed concerts I genuinely wanted to see and discovered others that rearranged my entire hierarchy of the weekend. Thursday: entering the festival through Denuit and A Projection My Castle Party began on Thursday evening with Denuit, and it was a beautiful way to enter the festival. Their concert had something dreamlike without becoming fragile or vague. The music carried a strong pulse, yet seemed to move through layers of light and atmosphere rather than simply pushing forward. The visual side was astonishing. Saturated colours altered the apparent dimensions of the stage, sometimes opening a wider space around the musicians and then suddenly enclosing it again. The lighting never felt like a decorative screen placed over the music. It created new rooms inside the songs and gave the performance an almost unreal depth while keeping the connection with the audience intact. There was elegance in the show, but there was also force. The melodies remained clear, while the electronics carried enough physical weight to hold the Park Stage. Denuit created a world remarkably quickly, and the audience entered it without needing much persuasion. A Projection followed and changed the temperature immediately. I had already seen them at Castle Party in the Club in Wrocław, where they made an excellent impression, and the Bolków performance confirmed how naturally their music expands on a larger stage. The guitars cut through the electronic pulse, and the whole set had a kinetic quality, as though every darker emotion had been pushed through a faster, more volatile circuit. Melancholy remained present, but the music refused to let it become passive. Even the Girls Under Glass cover felt fully absorbed into A Projection’s own language. It carried recognition, certainly, but it never became a museum piece offered politely to the scene. They respected its origin, then pulled it into their own speed and physical tension. Denuit and A Projection gave Thursday exactly the balance it needed. One created an immersive, almost enchanted atmosphere; the other sharpened it into motion. Later came another core part of Castle Party: the people. I had proper conversations with friends and acquaintances I had not seen for months, sometimes years, rather than rushed greetings exchanged while checking the time and calculating the distance to the next stage. Friday: the castle and an almost impossible lineup Friday was the day I had been waiting for most. The Castle Stage lineup was so strong that I remained there almost entirely, and it became my first real meeting with the castle during this edition. I arrived too late for The Last Digital Angel, which I regret, particularly because supporting the Polish representation was an important part of my festival plan. I did, however, reach the courtyard in time for She Pleasures Herself. They offered an engaging mixture of post-punk, gothic rock and darkwave without treating any of those references with excessive reverence. There was humour in the performance, good contact with the audience and a deliberate looseness that suited the afternoon slot very well. Rotersand Then came one of my major priorities: Rotersand. I had initially believed this was their first concert in Poland, but Krischan later corrected me. They had already played at Progresja in Warsaw many years ago, making Castle Party their second Polish appearance. Rotersand possess a particular kind of stage energy. It does not come from frantic movement or from trying to persuade the audience that every second is historic. Rascal and Krischan understand exactly how their songs function inside a crowd, and that confidence gives the music enough space to work without additional exaggeration. The set felt close to the best of what Rotersand can offer. The songs were immediate, sharp and immensely satisfying, with hooks that arrived quickly without ever feeling disposable. Rascal’s contact with the audience was direct and energetic, while Krischan held the electronic architecture together with precision. The audience had clearly been waiting for this concert. Rotersand delivered completely. Empathy Test Empathy Test changed the atmosphere without losing the audience’s attention. Isaac Howlett remarked that he had finally reached Castle Party, and seeing him on that stage genuinely felt right. His voice is central to the identity of the project, and the castle presented it with an interesting challenge. Empathy Test’s songs often feel private, close and emotionally exposed, while the courtyard is large and visually imposing. The performance found the right scale: drums and electronics gave the songs greater physical breadth, while Isaac’s voice remained intimate and immediately recognisable. It was a genuinely moving Castle Party debut. Hocico Then Hocico arrived, and the stage became a different organism. Hocico perform with the energy of a thunderstorm that has somehow developed intent. Erk entered wearing his familiar bone-like mask and began moving across the stage with reserves of physical energy that remain astonishing no matter how many times one witnesses them. Nothing about the performance felt cautious. The audience responded immediately. The courtyard became louder, rougher and less orderly, which was exactly what the music demanded. Hocico took possession of the crowd, and the crowd gave itself over willingly. Diary of Dreams: the forces of music and nature What a night. Diary of Dreams have occupied a very particular place in my life for more than 20 years. These songs have become part of the internal soundscape of many listeners, connected to losses, relationships, periods of solitude and private turning points. Diary of Dreams had already returned to Castle Party repeatedly, playing in 2003, 2007, 2009, 2011, 2017 and 2021. Their seventh Bolków appearance carried the weight of that long relationship. The music expanded inside the courtyard: electronics accumulated against the stone instead of disappearing into open air, while the guitars struck the walls and seemed to return enlarged, rougher and more physical. Adrian Hates’ voice retained its intimacy inside that scale. Then the forces of nature entered the same space as the forces of music. Rain swept across the courtyard, the wind cut through the stage, and some of the equipment had to be moved farther back before the concert could continue safely. Everyone was wet, cold and trying to protect cameras, clothes and whatever had not yet been soaked. Still, once the performance continued, the weather became inseparable from its image. Rain travelled through the lights, wind caught Adrian’s hair and threw it across his face, and the sound moved through the storm, struck the castle walls and returned to the people standing below. Then came “She and Her Darkness,” a complete heartbreaker every time. More than two decades of familiarity have produced no immunity whatsoever. Despite the profoundly cold circumstances, the welcome from Bolków was as warm as ever. Covenant: exactly the right band to inherit the night Covenant arrived in Bolków under circumstances nobody had wanted. VNV Nation had been forced to withdraw because of Ronan Harris’ health, leaving another band to enter a headlining slot already filled with expectation. Covenant were exactly the right band to inherit it. Every time I see Covenant, I am reminded how little they actually need around them. There are no fireworks and no enormous theatrical concept designed to make the concert appear larger than it is. Eskil Simonsson, Daniel Myer and Daniel Jonasson take their places, the music begins, and the scale establishes itself naturally. The set felt close to the best-of selection one secretly hopes to receive at a festival. The lighting was spectacular, among the most beautiful of the entire festival. Eskil has a rare way of speaking between songs – kind, intelligent, slightly poetic and occasionally philosophical – that makes a huge festival audience feel unexpectedly close. The encore gave Friday night the grand finale it needed. Covenant had entered a difficult position and transformed it into a complete Covenant concert: powerful, warm, intelligent and musically assured. Saturday: between the castle and a miniature industrial festival Saturday demanded more movement. I began at the Castle Stage, then ran towards the Park Stage, where the afternoon and evening gradually turned into a miniature industrial festival concealed within Castle Party. Her Own World My day began with Her Own World, and once again the band surprised me in the best possible way. The projections, costumes, choreography, lighting and music operated as one complete structure. Yu has grown enormously as a frontperson – she no longer seems to be negotiating with the scale of the production around her; she owns its centre. The heavier passages had genuine impact, guitars and electronics creating a solid foundation while melodic lines kept the music open and emotionally accessible. Among the Polish acts appearing at Castle Party this year, Her Own World delivered one of the most mature and fully realised performances. The Silverblack The Silverblack followed with an immediate visual statement: black-and-white makeup, a strongly metallic appearance and a presentation that suggested industrial gothic metal before the first song had fully settled. The musicians had very good contact with the audience, direct, energetic and often playful. Long Night The Norwegians from Long Night brought a different kind of darkness. The vocals were deep, dark and beautifully controlled, giving the songs a weight that required no additional theatre. Long Night’s strength came from tone, voice and the internal atmosphere of the material. In Slaughter Natives By the time I reached In Slaughter Natives, Saturday had begun to resemble a compact industrial festival hidden inside the larger Castle Party programme. Jouni Havukainen’s voice was astonishing. To say that he sang would describe only part of what occurred. The sound seemed to involve his whole body: breath, chest, posture, the contraction of his torso and the visible effort required to force each phrase outward. There was nothing easy in this performance: no attempt to charm the crowd, no softening of the material for a festival afternoon. XOTOX Then came XOTOX, and people, that was a fucking show – one of the strongest performances I saw at Castle Party. Andreas Davids performed with his wife, Claudia, and they needed remarkably little around them. Two tall structures carrying the XOTOX imagery, crosses, hard light, two people and the full physical force of the sound proved entirely sufficient. We also heard two brand-new pieces, both performed live for the first time. The most impressive part was the physical change in the audience. People began moving as one mass, responding immediately to each new impact. XOTOX were a fucking knockout. This Morn’ Omina I had not seen This Morn’ Omina in many, many years. The musicians stood behind electronic stations and drums arranged along long illuminated structures that looked almost like altars, while Mika Goedrijk occupied the centre – not simply fronting a band, but becoming the axis around which rhythm, movement, light and physical pressure were organised. It was a fucking blast. Percussion did not accompany the music; it set the conditions under which the audience experienced it. Visually, the whole thing stood out: blue, red and purple light travelled across the altar-like stations, drums, bodies and props, giving the stage a ceremonial quality without turning the concert into empty ritual theatre. Hybryds Hybryds brought my Saturday to a close by changing the state of attention completely. After the physical force of XOTOX and This Morn’ Omina, the performance slowed the nervous system without allowing it to relax fully. It was poetic, ritualistic and visually beautiful, an intelligent conclusion to Saturday. Sunday: Polish machinery, illuminated flowers and one enormous discovery Sunday was shorter for me, although it produced one of my greatest discoveries of the entire festival. Agonised Too I began with Agonised Too, and the immediate thought was: what a machine. Rafał Tomaszczuk’s delivery retained the damage, longing and inward tension present in the recorded material, met with impressive authority against a much larger sonic field. Bartosz Hervy constructed the electronic environment and controlled the visualisations behind them, among the most carefully integrated of the weekend. Rafał carried the exposed human centre, while Bartosz constructed the surrounding space. White Ritual White Ritual followed with a stage covered in illuminated flowers and carefully arranged decorations. The interaction between male and female vocals created the central tension of the set, with softness, desire and darker force passing through the same songs. HORSKH Then HORSKH happened. I had never seen them before, and I was completely unprepared for what their music would do to me. Live drums, electronics and guitars tore into one another like parts of the same overloaded machine. It was wild without becoming shapeless, ferocious without losing internal control. Then came The Prodigy cover. Hell yes. I entered the concert knowing almost nothing about HORSKH. I left with my ears, body and entire emotional system thoroughly ground through, yet somehow returned sharper, more awake and desperate to experience it again. They were one of my greatest discoveries and one of the defining performances of Castle Party 2026. Rue Oberkampf: my ending My Castle Party ended with Rue Oberkampf, one of my long-standing favourites. After HORSKH, their entrance did not reduce the intensity; it redirected it. They opened with “Hope and Fear,” the perfect beginning for my final concert. Onstage, the project understands the value of restraint: movement is limited enough for every gesture to register, while the lighting picks out the figures and then partially removes them again. Four days later Castle Party 2026 was never going to become a neat chain of perfectly witnessed concerts. There were unavoidable overlaps, bands I missed, rain, wind, technical interruptions, running between stages, cold clothes, physical exhaustion and constant decisions about where I needed to be next. Giving Castle Party all four days brought back something I had been missing. Thursday’s conversations remained present throughout the weekend, and people in the audience became recurring figures rather than anonymous faces. Bands that have lived with me for decades stood beside projects I encountered for the first time. I had also done the thing I thought might no longer be possible: I had taken all four days of Castle Party, and I am very glad that I did. About Castle Party Castle Party began on 20 August 1994 at Grodziec Castle. The first edition brought together around 300 people and five Polish bands near the beginning of their careers: Moonlight, Daimonion, T.R.H., Pornografia and Fading Colours. The festival grew quickly: around 800 people attended the two-day 1995 edition, and roughly 1,000 attended in 1996 with a larger programme. Grodziec could no longer comfortably contain the audience, so the fourth Castle Party moved to Bolków Castle in 1997, the setting with which it has remained identified since: an enclosed medieval courtyard, stone walls that alter the physical scale of the sound, and a small town temporarily taken over by the dark alternative scene. Attendance reached roughly 2,000 in 1998 and around 4,000 in 1999, when Clan of Xymox headlined a programme drawing visitors from Poland, Germany and the Czech Republic. Castle Party became a three-day event in 2000, presenting 34 bands from across Europe and opening a second stage for the first time. Side-Line reported on the full 2026 timetable when it was announced in May, ahead of this year’s four-day edition at Bolków from 16 to 19 July.

items.body: American darkwave duo Boy Harsher has signed to Atlantic Records and announced a new album, Get Mean, due September 18, 2026. The twelve-track release is the duo’s first full-length since the 2022 film and soundtrack “The Runner,” and their major-label debut. Alongside the announcement, Jae Matthews and Augustus Muller shared a new single, “Hard Beat,” with a self-directed video. GET MEAN by Boy Harsher “Get Mean” was recorded across eight locations in the United States, Mexico and Italy. The album traces Matthews and Muller’s process after the pair, formerly a couple, ended their romantic relationship in early 2024, a period that also brought family loss and creative uncertainty before the duo decided to continue Boy Harsher together. Matthews describes the record as “what I had to give during the most extreme period of my life.” Across its twelve tracks, “Get Mean” pairs Boy Harsher’s established coldwave propulsion with detuned pads, synth leads, pedal-steel parts, new wave guitar and phone-recorded fragments gathered during Matthews’s travels through West Texas, the Pacific Northwest and South Florida. Boy Harsher ‘Get Mean’ tracklist Ronny Jeans Break Me Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call) Faulty Coming Home Hard Beat Ice Pick (Walk Away) Ivy’s Spiral Pray 4 Me Falling ~ Bleed “Jeans,” released in June 2026, was the first track shared from the album. “Hard Beat” is the second single, built around a bass-synth figure, a steady kick drum and Matthews’s vocal. Its video, directed by Boy Harsher with cinematography by Owen Smith-Clark, follows two characters through a nighttime highway drive intercut with a closed-circuit surveillance narrative shot inside a tiled room. “Get Mean” is available to pre-order and pre-save on Bandcamp via Nude Club Records, the duo’s own imprint, through Atlantic Records. GET MEAN by Boy Harsher Boy Harsher 2026 tour dates Boy Harsher will support “Get Mean” with a North American headlining run beginning September 25 in Hudson, New York, followed by European and UK dates in November and December. The tour was first announced in June 2026 as “The Heartbreak Tour”; several North American dates are sold out. Support acts on select shows include Choir Boy, Evanora Unlimited, True Blue and Kassie Krut.
