Bristol, UK – Bristol Electric at SWX December 4 – Antwerp, Belgium – De Roma About Boy Harsher Boy Harsher formed in 2014 in Savannah, Georgia, where vocalist Jae Matthews and producer Augustus Muller met while studying film. The pair first worked together as Teen Dreamz in 2013, pairing Matthews’s spoken word with Muller’s electronics, before renaming the project Boy Harsher and releasing the home-recorded EP “Lesser Man” the same year; the track “Pain” spread widely online and became an early calling card for the duo. They later relocated to Northampton, Massachusetts. The duo released their debut album “Yr Body Is Nothing” in 2016 through DKA Records, followed by the “Country Girl” EP in 2017. In 2018 they founded their own label, Nude Club, and reissued earlier material through it. Their second album, “Careful,” arrived on February 1, 2019 via Nude Club Records, with a companion remix collection, “Careful Remixes, etc.,” issued the same year. Side-Line reviewed “Careful” in September 2019, noting the record’s 80s electro-pop and cold-wave influences and rating it 8½. In January 2022, Matthews and Muller released their directorial debut, the short film “The Runner,” with an accompanying soundtrack, and followed it with festival appearances including Primavera Sound, Roadburn and Coachella. In November 2024, the duo featured on Pet Shop Boys’ double A-side single “New London Boy / All The Young Dudes,” while Muller continued his side project Safe Mind with Cooper B. Handy. Boy Harsher are also directing and scoring an upcoming feature-length horror thriller, “The Lonely Woman,” starring Chloe Sevigny, FKA twigs, Sturgill Simpson, Will Oldham and Jake Weary. In June 2026, Boy Harsher announced “The Heartbreak Tour,” their first extended North American headlining run since the 2022 “The Runner” cycle. With “Get Mean,” announced in July 2026 and due September 18 via Atlantic Records, that tour becomes the album’s launch run, extending into Europe and the UK through December.

items.body: British electro-industrial group Portion Control have released “H.O.T. Matter (Demo version 1)“, the third single from their archival box set “1983-86 – Hit The Pulse to Purge…“, out 14 August 2026 on Artoffact Records. The set collects the London group’s mid-1980s work across a 4xCD box, a digital edition and a limited red vinyl LP. You can stream and pre-order the box set through the Bandcamp player below. 1983-86 – Hit The Pulse to Purge… by Portion Control Portion Control detail ‘H.O.T. Matter’ and the box set This demo version of “H.O.T. Matter” is being made available for the first time; the finished studio version of the track appeared on “Psycho Bod Saves The World”, Portion Control’s third studio album, released in 1986. A video accompanies the single. “It is strange and satisfying in equal measure to have this era of our catalogue finally gathered into a single coherent release,” the band state about the box set. It is an opportunity for long term and new listeners to hear the music of this period in full context. This material shaped our sound and attitude for all that has followed since. The box set, “1983-86 – Hit The Pulse to Purge…”, gathers 77 tracks. It brings together the 1983 mini-LP “Hit The Pulse”, the albums “..Step Forward” (1984) and “Psycho Bod Saves The World” (1986), the 12-inch singles “The Great Divide”, “Go-Talk” and “Raise The Pulse”, and the “Purge” EP (1986), alongside B-sides, compilation tracks, rarities, remixes, demos and two live recordings from 1984 and 1985. Paul Lavigne remastered all 77 tracks at Kontrast Mastering; 16 are previously unreleased and a further 12 appear on CD and digitally for the first time. The 4xCD edition comes in a five-panel ecopak with a 24-page booklet designed by Stefan Alt of Ant-Zen, and the red vinyl LP carries ten key tracks. “H.O.T. Matter” follows “Refugee (Rhys Fulber Rebuild)”, a version reworked by Rhys Fulber of Front Line Assembly, and “Tex-Mex (Live at Dolce Vita, Lausanne 6/12/85)”, the second single from the box set. Both original studio versions appeared on the 1984 album “..Step Forward”, which the group promoted on tour with Depeche Mode and Blancmange. Portion Control tour dates for 2026 and 2027 Portion Control have confirmed two festival appearances: 24 October 2026 – Zwickau, Germany – Elektrisch Festival 1-4 July 2027 – Canterbury, UK – Shadowlands Festival About Portion Control Portion Control formed in London in 1979 and built a raw, minimal sound around sequenced synthesisers, samplers and strident vocals. Their early records – the 1982 debut album “I Staggered Mentally”, the “Hit The Pulse” mini-LP (1983) and the second album “..Step Forward” (1984) – placed them among the pioneers of hard-edged electronic dance music, and the group supported Depeche Mode on tour in 1984. Their use of early sampling and drum-machine technology fed into the work of later acts including Nitzer Ebb, Skinny Puppy, Front Line Assembly, Nine Inch Nails and Orbital. After a hiatus that began in the late 1980s, Portion Control returned in 2004 with “Wellcome”, followed by “Filthy White Guy” (2006), “Pure Form” (2012) and the run of “SEED” EPs between 2020 and 2025. The group signed to Artoffact Records in late 2025, and the label is now reissuing their catalogue as a series of box sets. “1983-86 – Hit The Pulse to Purge…” is the first of those sets, and “H.O.T. Matter” is the third single drawn from it, following the band’s confirmed appearance at Zwickau’s Elektrisch Festival later this year.

The album opens with a powerful composition that recalls Industrial and Goth-Metal, immediately showcasing Thalie Némésis’s enchanting voice. As the record unfolds, it gradually reveals calmer and, above all, more dreamlike pieces, although several of them are punctuated by explosive, heavier climaxes. Her Ethereal vocals act as a guiding force, leading the listener like a mermaid—or perhaps a muse—through a magical sonic landscape. The floating, atmospheric passages often evolve into something almost Cinematic. Towards the end, a growing sense of foreboding takes hold, culminating in a mystical and captivating closing track. Above all, Thalie Némésis is an artist with a distinctive artistic identity—something I find far more compelling than the work of those who simply rely on a predictable ‘copy-and-paste’ formula. (Rating:7). Side-Line covered the release of “Dé(s)figurations” when it came out on Meridian Noir Records in May 2026. Listen to “Ruptures”: Ruptures by Thalie Némésis About Thalie Némésis Thalie Némésis is the solo project of the French musician Nathalie, based in Aix-en-Provence. The project first appeared in 2013 and released early material in 2014, including work with Les Modules Étranges, before a long pause. Thalie Némésis returned with the 2025 EP “Catarsi Apotropaica,” which forms the first half of “Dé(s)figurations.” Nathalie co-founded Meridian Noir Records, a French label for dark alternative music, with Albin Wagener of The Memory of Snow, whose album “Inside” the label released in June 2026. “Dé(s)figurations,” out May 22, 2026 on Meridian Noir, is reviewed above.

items.body: Mängelexemplar (MNGLXMPLR) has been active for 15 years, steadily winning over fans with its distinctive synth-driven sound. On this latest album, the German duo—Lilli B. and Joa H.—presents eleven brand-new tracks. The title track, which also serves as the opener, is a brilliant composition that perfectly embodies the spirit of Minimal-Wave and Electro. Highly danceable, it combines fantastic synth work, robotic vocals, and unmistakable Kraftwerk-inspired textures. In my opinion, it ranks among the finest Electro tracks released in recent years—a genuine masterpiece. While the remaining songs may not quite reach the same extraordinary level, the album consistently delivers music of the highest quality. The warm vintage production and classic 80s drum machine rhythms evoke a powerful sense of nostalgia, yet MNGLXMPLR effortlessly transform these influences into a fresh, contemporary sound where minimalism meets meticulous craftsmanship. Subtle EBM elements occasionally surface, and a few darker compositions add extra depth, but the album never loses its focus or momentum. The closing track, sung in English, provides a welcome contrast to the predominantly German-language material. “Neue Zukunft” is an exceptionally accomplished release, with every element perfectly balanced. It is a remarkable album that deserves to be discovered by anyone with a passion for classic Electro, Minimal-Wave, and intelligent Electronic music. (Rating:9). Listen to “Neue Zukunft”: Neue Zukunft by Mängelexemplar About Mängelexemplar Mängelexemplar (MNGLxMPLR) is a synth wave duo from Düsseldorf, Germany, active since 2011. The lineup comprises Lilli B. on lyrics and vocals and Joa H. (Joachim Saleina) on synthesizers, rhythm machines, and vocals. The duo releases through Infacted Recordings and its own imprint, Carisma Studios. Their previous full-length, “Non Plus Ultra,” appeared in 2020. Mängelexemplar previewed the follow-up with the singles “Hochhausdach,” “Mängelexemplar,” “Neue Zukunft,” and “Kontraste” before Infacted Recordings released the “Neue Zukunft” album digitally on March 27, 2026, with Carisma Studios issuing a limited 12-inch vinyl edition. That album, reviewed above, is the duo’s first full-length release since “Non Plus Ultra.”

items.body: Kaderim ellerinde Paslı bir kafeste Ruhum uçmak ister Masum bir hevesle After a two-year absence, London-based Turkish musician Affet Robot returned with three songs tracing a tightening path from ruin to confinement. The sequence began with Kan ve Kül (“Blood and Ash”), continued with Tuzak (“Trap”), and now reaches its conclusion with Kafes (“Cage”), an ensnaring darkwave track built for the dancefloor while its words search desperately for a way out. Kafes opens on an organ-like low-end synth hum before a volley of rounded FM tones rolls in and rapid percussion gathers underneath. A bright, insistent guitar melody soon takes hold; later, bell-like synth notes ring through the arrangement. Bass and sequenced electronics maintain a spring-loaded dark groove throughout its four-minute runtime, while reverbed guitars widen the space around them. Eren Günsan’s Turkish vocal sits deep within layers of echo, giving his delivery a mechanical, distant quality—as if his voice is already reaching the listener from behind the song’s four walls. The lyrics place fate in another person’s hands. Günsan sings of a soul longing to fly from a rusted cage, only to find itself caught in a net by “sweet poison,” with no visible exit and the key held elsewhere. The closing lines turn the cage inward: the same cycle repeats, four walls return, and each attempt to retreat into the self brings another wave of nausea. Where Tuzak named the condition, Kafes gives it walls. The lyric video folds live footage filmed at London’s Nambucca into saturated red, green, and violet light, keeping Günsan partly in silhouette as he performs amid smoke and severe beams of colour. Jagged Caligari-style lyrics cut across the screen, turning the stage image into a moving enclosure that reflects the song’s circling thoughts. Watch the video for Kafes below: Affet Robot is the music project of Eren Günsan, a musician born and raised in Turkey and currently based in London. Drawing from darkwave and post-punk, the project combines cold electronic textures, reverberant guitars, propulsive rhythms, and Turkish-language songwriting into a distinct identity within the international darkwave scene. Kafes was written, produced, and recorded in South London by Eren Günsan. Mixing was handled by Barış Ergün, with mastering by Gianni Peri. Its visual identity brings together cover photography by Gökay Çatak, artwork by Öykü Özünal, and promotional photographs shot in London by Barış Uçar. Listen to Kafes below and order the single here. items.body: Cult Epics is celebrating the work of Rozz Williams this summer in three parts: a new three-track Flowers 12-inch, a feature-length documentary about the late Christian Death founder, and a Pomona concert featuring former members of the band alongside several of Williams’ longtime collaborators. Originally released on Rozz Williams and Gitane Demone’s 1995 collaborative album Dream Home Heartache, “Flowers” returns July 24 in a new three-track edition from Cult Epics. Available digitally and on limited-edition pink vinyl, the 12-inch pairs a new 2026 analog remix with remastered piano and live versions of the Williams composition, which also appears in director Nico B’s forthcoming documentary, Rozz Williams: Romeo’s Distress. The A-side features a 2026 analog remix built around Williams’ recorded vocal, with newly recorded instrumental parts by former Christian Death members Rikk Agnew on guitar, James McGearty on bass and David Glass on drums. Paul Roessler of 45 Grave contributes keyboards. Side B collects two additional versions of the song: a remastered piano rendition drawn from Williams and Gitane Demone’s Dream Home Heartache and a remastered live performance originally released on Sleeping Dogs. Flowers 12-inch tracklist: Side A: “Flowers” (Analog Version — Remix 2026) Side B: “Flowers” (Piano Version — Remastered 2026) Side B: “Flowers” (Live Version — Remastered 2026) The three-track record runs approximately 20 minutes and is priced at $20. The pink-vinyl edition carries the catalog number CE210 and is being distributed by MVD Entertainment Group. Listen to an excerpt of “Flowers” below: Rozz Williams: Romeo’s Distress The record arrives ahead of the August 29 screening of Rozz Williams: Romeo’s Distress at the Fox Theater Pomona. Billed as a homecoming in the city where Williams grew up, the event pairs Nico B’s documentary with an extended live performance by former Christian Death members and special guests. The 100-minute film examines Williams’ work as a musician, poet and visual artist, as well as his role in founding Christian Death and shaping the sound and imagery of Los Angeles deathrock. Williams died in 1998 at the age of 34, leaving behind a body of work that extended through Christian Death, Shadow Project, Premature Ejaculation and numerous collaborations. Watch the trailer for Rozz Williams: Romeo’s Distress below: Former Christian Death Members to Perform in Pomona Following the screening, Agnew, McGearty and Glass will take the stage with vocal performances by Eva O and Gitane Demone. The night also will feature appearances by Patrik Mata of Kommunity FK, Roessler, William Faith of Shadow Project and Williams’ collaborator Kenton Holmes. The extended set will draw from the three Christian Death albums recorded with Williams — Only Theatre of Pain, Catastrophe Ballet and Ashes — together with selections from Shadow Project. Rozz Williams: Romeo’s Distress — Documentary Screening and Live Performance Saturday, August 29, 2026 — 7 p.m. Fox Theater Pomona 301 S. items.body: I've been writing for a while about the injection of ideas and sounds from shoegaze, indie, and alternative rock into post-rock and metal. I mean, the process has been going for decades now but it seems that another wave has hit us in the last two years or so. What I've yet to hear though is a doom band incorporating these same influences. On Cycles in the Infinite Dream, REZN appear to have done just that. While the bedrock of their sound is still there, namely thick guitar chords over dreamy atmosphere conjured forth by synths and evocative vocals, the flavor feels wholly different. The guitars are not as dominant and the structure of the tracks is less concerned with crushing as it is with unfurling. As a result, the atmospheric elements of REZN's sound take precedence and blend with ideas from the aforementioned genres.This is all great stuff by the way, if you were having doubts on where I stand. Cycles in the Infinite Dreams is the band's sixth release (depending on how you count) and comes on the heels of the excellent and successful Solace and Burden. While I adore those releases (and their earlier ones are also great), it's fantastic to hear something new from the band. "The Vessel" is probably my favorite track on the album. It showcases the new melodical layout of the album in a great way. It opens with a classic REZN riff, all doomy groove and presence. But along the halfway mark, we can find a chorus resplendent in a more somber guitar lead and adorned with a grungier, more melancholic main riff. Add in the vocals in a new, "thinner" mode (which is not a criticism, rather a description) and the picture coalesces into something new, more contemplative and open ended than the band's previous sound. This is capitulated upon a bit later with a passage I can compare to no one else but Karnivool.Like I mentioned above, the heaviness is still there for those of you who are worried. Check out "Cloudfall" for example and its extremely kick-ass main riff. The guitars and bass still know how to go when REZN want them to, delivering thick, redolent doom metal when the band want them too. In fact, I think Cycles in the Infinite Dream has some of the band's best riffs, perhaps due to the fact that they have more freedom, and obligation, to play around with how they are constructed. But on this track as well, the presence is not maintained throughout the track but rather used as just another element in the sound.The end result of all of this is an album that might disappoint any REZN conservatives out there (is that even a thing?) If you're looking for Burden 2.0, this is not that and I, for one, am very happy about that. I want REZN, who are one of my favorite doom metal bands in operation, to keep pushing their sound and see what else they have to say. On Cycles in the Infinite Dream, it seems as if they have plenty left in their vocabulary. The album shines with a fresh approach, one that is happy to jump into the current direction that many (if not all) bands in the space are taking. Cycles in the Infinite Dream by REZN

items.body: Top PicksRezn – Cycles In The Infinite Dream (post-prog)If Cycles In The Infinite Dream had come out before we posted our Top 25 Albums of the Year So Far lists, it probably would have topped mine. This comes as a shock to me as much as it might to some of you. Previously, Rezn have professed a sludgier, doomier product. Here, though, they've taken a turn for more progressive pastures, resulting in a both a lighter and more engaging sound. Elder's Through Zero provides a popular point of comparison. However, there's also an almost uplifting, elated mournfulness to proceedings that reminds me of the first (superior) Pallbearer album, or even Pink Floyd, during its floatier sections—except they also throw a big, stonking Mastodon-style sludge-riff on the end of every other song as well. Fantastic stuff! Cycles in the Infinite Dream by REZN Sallow Moth – Hydrophilous Blood (weird prog-death)This is some very good, weird prog-death. items.album: 岡本太郎がやったこと
items.excerpt: 岡本太郎（1911–1996）の思想と芸術は、一見バラバラに見える複数の要素を強く結びつける。シュールレアリスム、変性意識（あるいは無意識・呪術的体験）、縄文時代、東北文化、沖縄文化は、彼にとって「近代合理主義が抑圧した根源的な生命力」を取り戻すための、連続した探究の軌跡だった。以下、それぞれを丁寧に追いながら、相互の関係を整理する。 続きをみる

items.album: ホルヘ・ルイス・ボルヘス

1899年8月24日ブエノスアイレス生まれ、1986年6月14日ジュネーヴにて86歳で死去。アルゼンチンの短編作家、随筆家、詩人、翻訳家、図書館員であり、20世紀のスペイン語文学および世界文学の中心的人物の一人です。彼の作品は幻想文学、哲学的文学、ポストモダニズム、マジック・リアリズムの形成に深く影響を与えました。家族背景と幼少期ボルヘスは教育のある中流階級の家庭に生まれました。父はホルヘ・ギジェルモ・ボルヘス・ハスラム（Jorge Guillermo Borges Haslam）。弁護士で心理学教師、小説『エル・カウディーリョ』（1921）を書いた文学志望者でもあり、哲学的アナーキスト（スペンサーの弟子）でした。母はレオノール・アセベド・スアレス（Leonor Acevedo Suárez）。古くからのアルゼンチン・ウルグアイ系の家系で、翻訳も手がけ、敬虔なカトリックでした。妹は画家のノラ・ボルヘス。父方祖母はイギリス人（フランセス・ハスラム）で、家庭では英語とスペイン語が話され、ボルヘスは英語をスペイン語より先に読みました。父の膨大な英語・スペイン語蔵書（千冊超）が「人生最大の出来事」だったと本人が述べています。幼少期に読んだのはマーク・トウェイン、エドガー・アラン・ポー、ヘンリー・ワズワース・ロングフェロー、ロバート・ルイス・スティーヴンソン、H.G.ウェルズ、セルバンテスの『ドン・キホーテ』（英語版で先に）、『千夜一夜物語』など。7歳頃から書き始め、9歳でオスカー・ワイルドの「幸福な王子」をスペイン語に翻訳して新聞に掲載されました。父は「文学の運命を息子が果たすべき」と暗黙に期待していました。1914年、父の視力治療のため一家はスイス・ジュネーヴへ。ボルヘスはコレジ・ド・ジュネーヴで学び、フランス語・ラテン語を習得、独学でドイツ語を学び、ドイツ哲学や表現主義詩人を読みました。第一次世界大戦のためヨーロッパ滞在が延び、1919年頃からスペインへ。マヨルカ、セビージャ、マドリードを経て、ウルトラ主義（Ultraísmo）の前衛運動に参加。1921年にブエノスアイレスへ帰国し、ウルトラ主義を南米に紹介しました。文学活動の展開帰国後、詩誌『プリスマ』や『プロア』を創刊。1923年に処女詩集『ブエノスアイレスの情熱』（Fervor de Buenos Aires）を刊行。初期はブエノスアイレスを歌う詩や随筆を書き、マケドニオ・フェルナンデスやビクトリア・オカンポの『スール』誌に関わりました。アドルフォ・ビオイ・カサーレスとの親交が始まり、後に共同でH.ブストス・ドメス名義の探偵小説・パロディを書きました。1930年代に入ると、非現実性や存在論的な問いを扱う方向へ。1935年『世界の汚辱史』（Historia universal de la infamia）で、歴史上の悪漢の伝記を再話・捏造する形の作品を発表。1938年に父が死去し、自身もクリスマス・イブに頭部に重傷を負い、敗血症で死の淵をさまよいました。この経験が創作の転機となり、1939年の「ピエール・メナール、ドン・キホーテの著者」など、メタフィクション的な短編が生まれます。1940年代に代表作が集中します。1941年『分岐する小径の庭』（El jardín de senderos que se bifurcan）、1944年にそれを拡充した『フィクションズ』（Ficciones）、1949年『アレフ』（El Aleph）。これらが彼の核心です。視力は1920年代から徐々に衰え、1927年頃から複数回の手術を受け、1950年代後半にはほぼ全盲となりました（遺伝性で、父や祖母も盲目）。点字は習わず、母や秘書の助けで口述し、暗記に頼りました。1955年にペロン政権崩壊後、国立図書館館長に就任（1973年ペロン復帰時に辞任）。ブエノスアイレス大学で英米文学を教授。主要作品短編集 • 『世界の汚辱史』（1935）：非フィクション風の再話と偽作。 • 『分岐する小径の庭』（1941）→『フィクションズ』（1944、1956改訂）：「バベルの図書館」「トレーン、ウクバール、オルビス・テルティウス」「分岐する小径の庭」「円環の廃墟」「ピエール・メナール」など。無限、迷宮、夢、架空の作家、可能性の分岐を扱います。 • 『アレフ』（1949）：「アレフ」（宇宙の一点にすべてが集約される）、「死とコンパス」「アステリオンの家」など。 • 『ブローディの報告書』（1970）、『砂の本』（1975）：「砂の本」（無限のページを持つ本）など後期作品。 • その他：『想像上の存在の書』（1967、マルガリータ・ゲレーロと共著）など。詩集 • 『ブエノスアイレスの情熱』（1923）、『正面の月』（1925）、『サン・マルティンのノート』（1929）。 • 後期：『影の賛美』（1969）、『虎の黄金』（1972）、『深い薔薇』（1975）、『共謀者たち』（1985）など。盲目をテーマにしたものが多い。随筆・評論 • 『探究』（1925）、『永遠の歴史』（1936）、『別の探究』（1952）など。時間、永遠、比喩、文学論。 • 英文学・ゲルマン文学・ダンテ論など多数。ビオイ・カサーレスとの共同作（探偵小説シリーズ）や翻訳（フォークナーなど）も重要です。テーマ・スタイル・哲学モチーフは一貫して迷宮、鏡、夢、無限、図書館・アーカイブ、時間の循環・分岐、架空の書物・作家、神話の再解釈です。現実と虚構の境界をぼかし、形而上学的な遊びを行います。理想主義（バークリー）、ショーペンハウアー、スピノザ、カフカ、ポー、スティーヴンソン、東洋思想（仏教・道教）などの影響が強い。哲学を物語として体感させる手法が特徴で、読者に概念を先に経験させます。ポストモダン文学の先駆者・実践者ともされ、メタフィクション、自己言及的テキスト、ジャンル混淆を徹底しました。マジック・リアリズムへの影響も大きく、ガルシア＝マルケスらラテンアメリカ文学の道を開いたと評価されます。数学的概念（集合論など）を文学に取り入れた点も指摘されます。視力喪失と晩年全盲後も口述で創作・講演を続け、母が秘書役を長く務めました（母は99歳まで生きた）。1967年に若い頃交際したエルサ・アステテ・ミジャンと結婚（3年ほどで破綻、母の勧めが大きかった）。その後、助手で後の妻となるマリア・コダマと長年行動を共にし、1986年にパラグアイで結婚（アルゼンチンの離婚法回避のため）。コダマは遺産の唯一の相続人となり、死後も財団を通じて作品を管理しました。政治的にはペロン政権を強く嫌悪（リベラルで反権威主義的傾向から）。ペロン時代に図書館職を降格させられた経験もあり、反ペロニズムが鮮明でした。1976年の軍政には一時支持を示しましたが、全体として「政治は信じない」「美学と哲学に関心する」と述べています。受賞・評価・遺産1961年にフォルメントール賞（サミュエル・ベケットと共同）を受賞し、国際的に一気に認知されました。その後、フランス芸術文学勲章、イギリスの名誉KBE、エルサレム賞、セルバンテス賞（1980）など多数。ノーベル文学賞は長年候補に挙がりながら受賞しませんでした。影響は広範で、ポストモダニズム、マジック・リアリズム、哲学者（フーコー、ローティ、ウンベルト・エーコなど）、作家（ジョン・バース、デイヴィッド・フォスター・ウォレスなど）に及びます。「近代とポストモダンの橋渡し」と評されることもあります。ジュネーヴで肝臓癌により死去。埋葬はジュネーヴのプレーンパレ墓地。墓石にはアングロサクソン・古ノルドの彫刻が施されています。最後まで「正しい言葉」を迷宮の中で探すような精神でいました。ボルヘスの作品は短編中心で、長編小説をほとんど書いていません。本人は「小説を書く才能がない」と述べ、短く凝縮された形式を好みました。読む者に無限の解釈を開く「迷宮」そのもののような文学を残しました。続きをみる

items.body: 会期：2026/05/01～2026/06/28 会場：市原湖畔美術館［千葉県］ 公式サイト：https://lsm-ichihara.jp/exhibition/kotatakeuchi_kurayami/ 千葉県・市原湖畔美術館で「暗闇をくぐってみたら Part1」として竹内公太の個展「のののののまつり」が開催された。2026年秋まで改修が続く施設の入り口を暗幕が覆い、その奥の通常よりも限られたスペースに作品が展開する企画展である。タイトルに含まれる「のの」「の」は、太陽や月、仏などの尊いものを表わす幼児語の「ののさま」や「野」にちなむといい、自然や畏怖すべき存在に関わる展示であることが示唆されている。 竹内は本展へ参加するにあたり、市原市で4ヶ月におよぶフィールドワークを行ない、その際に撮影した石像や石碑、風景をもとに映像インスタレーションを制作している。東日本大震災をきっかけに福島県に移住した彼は、これまでも場所との関わりを基礎とする制作を行なってきた。本展でもその姿勢を引き継ぐとともに、赤く光る誘導棒や石碑といった前作までに扱ってきたモチーフを採用し、市原の自然や歴史と向き合う作品を展開している。 ［筆者撮影］ 最初の一室《三面世界へ》は空間全体がひとつの作品となっている。半分の壁面に6つの縦型の映像フレームが並び、そのすべてに三面馬頭観音が肖像画のように映されている。フレーム数やフレームレートの変更によってか、いずれもが微動し続け、アニメーションの語源となったアニミズムの印象を喚起させる。もう半分の壁には三面馬頭の視点を示すかのように、3つのプロジェクターによって屋外の風景が映されている。空、野焼きの火、月、鳥のはばたきなど、市原の風景を馬頭観音の視点から眺めるような構成である。 本展で扱われた石像や天体の撮影場所は、会場で配布されたリーフレットに記載されている。それによると市内を縦断する養老川をたどるように天空や馬頭観音が捉えられ、農耕や運搬を支えた馬との生活と、水との関わりが潜像するかのようだ。 ［筆者撮影］ 次のスペースには写真作品と、階段と宙空を挟むために近くまで行くことができない場所にプロジェクションされた夜空の映像がある。《十九+1夜》と題されたその映像は、新月から19日目の夜に女性たちが集う民間信仰の月待講「19夜」に注目したもので、その翌夜にあたる「20夜」に撮影され、次の集まりを待つ月の様子を示すという。 月待講や子安講は、安産や子育てについて祈念する女性たちの集会場として機能していたが近年では希少なものとなっている★1。ここでも映像の速度が変更され、月はせわしなく現われては去り、しばらくするとまた姿を現わす。その動きはどことなくユーモラスで、人とは異なる天体の時間感覚を表わし、会合が行なわれる時節を窺うようにして月は何度も展示室をめぐる。 ［筆者撮影］ 階段を降りた先が最後のスペースとなり、そこには20体の板貼りされた子安像の写真が座椅子に固定され、ほぼ等間隔に床置きされていた。子育てに関わる集いである子安講が石像たちによって形づくられ、そのうちの数体は映像モニターを眺めるかのように配置されている。映像には石碑が映り、それらは市内にある忠魂碑だという。石碑は時折クローズアップされ、「Loyal」「Age」といった英語字幕によっても漢字の意味を際立たせている。 ［筆者撮影］ 忠魂碑は日露戦争後に在郷軍人会を主体として建てられ、戦争で亡くなった人を悼むと同時に国家への忠誠を顕彰する性格を持つ。そのため敗戦後は新たに作られず、戦争犠牲者を悼む石碑を新設する場合には平和祈念碑などの呼称が使われた。戦意を称揚する遺物として破壊されることもあったようだが、第二次世界大戦の戦死者の名前を追記し、そのまま現在残るものも多い。建立時から現在に至るまでに石碑の意味合いが変容し、死者を生じさせる戦意高揚と死者を悼む哀悼という複層的な性質をはらむ。 本作《テレビのある集会所》のすぐ手前には、別の石碑を写した1枚の写真《国民精神総動員記念碑》が展示されている。「国民精神総動員」は日中戦争が始まってすぐに掲げられた国家政策で、国家への忠誠を証として示すことを促し、市原市では1938年に建立された。《テレビのある集会所》は、国策とともに顕現した1900年代に建てられた戦争に関わる石碑を、それよりもさらに古く建てられた子安像の共同体が囲み、眺める構成となっている。 本展は市原市に根づく民間信仰や子育てのコミュニティに注目し、馬頭観音像、子安像、忠魂碑といった石を介した歴史の継承に焦点を当てている。とくに国が軍事への傾斜を強める現在において、子の成育を祈念する子安像が子を喪失した記録でもある忠魂碑を見つめる様子は、地続きの歴史における出来事を過去から見返す視座であり、鑑賞者はその構造を自身が立つ現在地から望むことになる。 ［筆者撮影］ 歴史を伝えるメディアとして石を扱う竹内の視点は、東日本大震災での出来事──1933年の昭和三陸津波において設置された「津波記念石」が、70年代の道路工事で埋められたのち、2011年の震災で姿を現わす──を経て、より強く作品に表われるようになった★2。石像や石碑は丈夫なようで、それを保つための労力がなければ、自然に同化して姿を消す。現在、市原市では石造物や忠魂碑が人の手によって保たれているものの、身近ではなくなった子安講を石像が代替する様子は、その営みが永続的ではないことを思い出させる。 入り口と出口が同じ本展は会場をめぐったあと、最後は再び第一室の《三面世界へ》を経て美術館の外へと向かう。竹内は企画展のテーマである「暗闇をくぐってみたら」を反転的に捉え、作品群を暗幕の先の異世界として提示するのでなく、暗闇に包まれた馬頭観音の自然観をくぐったのちに、現実世界へ進み出る構造に注目する。土地や自然とともに形成されてきた人と石像との関わりを介して、現代社会へと視点を戻すことが促される展覧会だった。 鑑賞日：2026/05/19（火） ★1──会期中に開催されたトークイベントで登壇者の丸氏と会場参加者が、子安講が減少に向かう状況について述べている。 「大放談『市原にアナザーワールドはあるのか？』」レポート URL=https://lsm-ichihara.jp/blog/event2_kota_takeuchi/ ★2──「データが石になるとき」竹内公太『活動記録誌 “TkKt”』（トーキョーアーツアンドスペース、2023、74頁） URL=https://tokyocontemporaryartaward.jp/en/publication/2021-2023/takeuchi.pdf

items.excerpt: 東京・北千住BUoYにて、SFを主軸とするメディアanon pressによる新作書籍『TOKYO CYBERPUNK TRIBUTE』のリリースパーティが開催されます。 本イベントでは、2日間にわたって『TOKYO CYBERPUNK TRIBUTE』のテーマである「サイバーパンク」を軸に、計13組のアーティストによるライブアクトやDJに加え、VJや展示、パフォーマンス、トークなどが行なわれる予定です。 イベントの詳細は、下記および公式サイトをご覧ください。 『TOKYO CYBERPUNK TRIBUTE』 出版：anon press サイズ：B5変形判、496ページ SFにおけるある種の定番でありながらも正面から探求されることの少なかった「東京」と「サイバーパンク」をテーマとし、現代におけるその可能性を検討する作品集です。 ［発行元ウェブサイトより］ ■ライブアクト ＜7月31日（金）＞ ・EYRIE、諭吉佳作/men、kidlit、灰街令、Shuta Hiraki ＜8月1日（土）＞ ・r0tten、lil peace、MON/KU、HAIZAI AUDIO、JACKSON ka

items.body: ジャコモ・バッラ《鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム》 1912年、キャンバス・油彩、89.9×109.9cm、米国ニューヨーク州、バッファローAKG美術館蔵 Photo: Bridgeman Images / DNPartcom 無許可転載・転用を禁止   スピードの残像 FIFAワールドカップ2026が行なわれている（6/11-7/19）。48カ国が参加し、アメリカ・カナダ・メキシコの3カ国で開催される史上初の大会。テレビでは連日、世界のトッププレイヤーの華麗な足技がライブで実況放送されている。日本は残念ながらあのサッカー王国ブラジルに1対2で逆転負けしたが、大会を重ねるごとに世界の強豪国と渡り合えるチームへと成長を見せた。 明治時代に日本に伝えられたサッカーを漢字では蹴球（しゅうきゅう）と書くが、蹴球は日本に古くから伝わる遊技の蹴鞠（けまり）から名付けられたそうだ。蹴鞠は、飛鳥時代（644年頃）に中国から伝来し、日本独自の発展を遂げた宮廷貴族の遊びである。サッカーの絵ではないが、足元に注目した面白い絵があった。イタリアの画家ジャコモ・バッラの代表作《鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム》（米国ニューヨーク州、バッファローAKG美術館蔵）である。 黒い塊がふたつある抽象画かと一瞬思ったが、よく見るとスカートをはいた女性が犬を連れて散歩している絵だとわかってきた。淡いピンクを背景に靴底に緑、犬の足先には黄色を点じて、白から黒の濃淡を用い、透明感を出している。足元だけをクローズアップした不思議な絵。犬は全身が見え、女性は顔が見えないが、共に足が沢山ある。女性と犬をつなぐ金属質なリードが揺れて、女性も犬も足早に歩いているようだ。歩く瞬間の動作の残像を定着させて、スピード感や風や音など感覚を触発する。揺らぎを描いたマルセル・デュシャン（1887-1968）の《階段を降りる裸体No.2》（1912、フィラデルフィア美術館蔵）を想起させるが、バッラは何を描いたのだろうか。イタリア近現代美術史を専門としている太田岳人氏（以下、太田氏）に《鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム》の見方を伺いたいと思った。 太田氏は未来派を中心にイタリア近現代美術史を研究されており、千葉大学などで講師を務めている。博士論文「イタリア・ファシズム政権期の未来派 ──1930年代を中心に」を書かれ、未来派に所属していたバッラについても詳しい。千葉大学のあるJR西千葉駅前の喫茶店でお話を伺った。 毛利嘉孝氏 政治史から美術史へ 太田氏は、1979年愛知県岡崎市に生まれ、両親と弟と妹の5人家族で育った。絵を描くのが苦手で、歴史とファミコンゲーム好きの子供時代を過ごし、中学校では吹奏楽部に入り、高校では合唱部に所属した。音楽でイタリアの曲や歌に親しんでいたが、政治や外交の歴史に関心があり、1999年千葉大学文学部史学科に入学。イタリア・ルネサンスおよびマニエリスム美術を専門とする若桑みどり先生と出会い、太田氏は美術史の世界へ誘われていった。 「あらゆるジャンルの芸術家を糾合しつつ、情報発信やパフォーマンスを通じて、イタリア社会総体の革新へと進出しようとした壮大な文化運動であった未来派は、第一次世界大戦のような現実の戦争も“美”の領域に含め、1920年代以降は台頭するファシズム勢力にも接近している」と、政治史を勉強しようとしていた太田氏に未来派は興味深い謎に見えたという。 2001年に若桑先生が定年を迎え、群馬県立近代美術館の学芸課長でイタリア美術史を専門としていた上村清雄先生が2002年に着任し、太田氏は指導を受けるようになり、2010年ローマ大学へ1年間留学した。2013年博士論文を提出し、千葉大学大学院社会文化科学研究科の博士課程を修了。 太田氏が未来派の実物作品を自覚的に見たのは、2007年に初めてイタリアへ行ったときだった。未来派創立100周年記念展「Futurismo 100」など、各地で未来派展が開催された2009年にもイタリアで作品を見ていたが、未来派に関わる全体を研究対象とする太田氏にとって、当時の《鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム》の記憶は曖昧だという。 未来派の力動性 ジャコモ・バッラは、1871年7月18日イタリア北西部の州都トリノで生まれた。父を早くに亡くし、母は仕立て業を営む。バッラは、少年時代からリトグラフ制作の助手として働いた。トリノ美術学校の予科・本科で学び、1891年美術学校を中退して写真家オレステ・ベルティエーリ（1870–1908）のスタジオに職を得る。当時、先端的な画法であった分割主義を知り、「トリノ美術振興協会」の展覧会に初出品した。 1895年には母とローマへ移り、制作の拠点とする。イラストレーター、風刺画家、肖像画家として活動し、1899年にはヴェネツィア・ビエンナーレや、ローマの「美術愛好家・研究家協会」の国際美術展に作品を出品した。1900年にはパリで7カ月間過ごし、感覚的な印象派の絵画を、科学的な色彩理論に基づいて発展させた新印象主義の影響を受け、点描を用いる分割主義の画家として活動を始める。1902年、後に“未来派”の同志となる、ウンベルト・ボッチョーニ（1882-1916）やジーノ・セヴェリーニ（1883-1966）に分割主義の絵画技法を指導する。1904年エリーザ・マルクッチと結婚し、後に芸術家となる二人の娘ルーチェとエリカが誕生する。 未来派とは元来、電光・機械・ダイナミズム・速度といった現代文明が生み出した要素を強く肯定し、美術の枠を越えてあらゆる文化領域への浸透を試みた20世紀最初のアヴァンギャルド運動。キュビスムの影響があるとみられる一方、ダダイズムの先駆ともみられ、1909年イタリアの詩人フィリッポ・トンマーゾ・マリネッティ（1876-1944）が『フィガロ』紙に発表した「未来派創立宣言」によって始まった。同年バッラはパリのサロン・ドートンヌに出品した。 1910年ボッチョーニ、セヴェリーニ、カルロ・カッラ（1881-1966）、ルイージ・ルッソロ（1885-1947）と共に「未来派絵画技術宣言」に署名する。彼らの創造的表現とは、20世紀初頭の急速に変化する産業時代のダイナミズム（力動性）を体現するものであるべきだ、という点にあった。「あらゆるものが動き、走り、素早く変化する。…（略）…網膜上でイメージが持続することにより、運動する物体は増殖し、変形し、連続して生起し、振動のように、空間の中を通過する。したがって疾走する馬の脚は4本ではなく20本であり、それらの動きは三角形をなす」（図録『未来派 1909-1944』p.115）と宣言した。1912年《鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム》を制作する。 具象と抽象、平面と立体を横断 バッラは1913年、ローマの未来派展に初出品し、「抽象的速度」シリーズを始め、抽象画が増えていく。1914年には彫刻の制作を初めて試み、ローマのスプロヴィエーリ画廊で開催された「第1回未来派自由展」で発表。また、未来派様式の家具のデザインや未来派の衣服のデザインも手掛け、「反中立服装宣言」を掲げた。 1915年画家・彫刻家、デザイナーでもあったフォルトゥナート・デペーロ（1892-1960）と共にマニフェスト「未来派的宇宙の再構成」を発表。異質な素材によるオブジェ制作への志向を表わした。そして同年ローマのアンジェレッリ画廊で初の個展を開催。1916年未来派を牽引していたボッチョーニが亡くなり、バッラは「ボッチョーニの拳」をデザインし、それを詩人のマリネッティが未来派指導本部の公式レターヘッドに採用した。1917年バレエ・リュスのローマ公演『花火』の舞台装置をデザイン。1918年「色彩宣言」を発表。ローマのブラガーリア芸術の家で個展を開く。 バッラは、1920年代から主な未来派展に出品したほか、室内装飾やデザインの領域でも活躍した。その後もイタリアの政治家ベニート・ムッソリーニのローマ進軍を題材にするなど、ファシズムに接近したりしながら、欧米各地で作品を発表し続けた。1931年には「未来派航空絵画宣言」の共同署名者になり、徐々に作品は具象的になっていった。1935年ローマのサン・ルカ美術アカデミーの会員に選出されたが、未来派からは離れ孤立し始める。1947年ニューヨーク近代美術館（MoMA）から作品購入の打診があり、1949年《車の速度》《燕の飛行：線の展開＋ダイナミックな連続》がMoMAに所蔵された。バッラは1958年3月1日にローマにて死去、ローマのヴェラーノ墓地に眠る。享年87歳。 機械や暴力的な要素の未来派からは距離を置いたバッラ。具象と抽象、平面と立体を横断し、光と運動、そして速度を、色彩と幾何学的な抽象表現により詩的かつ機知に富んだ手法でイタリア未来派を切り開いてきた。   鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズムの見方 ①タイトル 鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム（くさりにつながれたいぬのだいなみずむ）。英題：Dynamism of a dog on a leash ②モチーフ 犬、鎖、女性の足。   ③制作年 1912年。バッラ41歳。   ④画材 キャンバス・油彩。   ⑤サイズ 縦89.9×横109.9cm。   ⑥構図 鎖をつけた犬と一緒に歩く女性の足元を真横からとらえた大胆な構図。   ⑦色彩 黒、ピンク、グレー、黄、紫、緑、赤茶、白など多色。一見色数が少なく見えるが、細部には繊細で輝くような色彩が付加されている。   ⑧技法 1882年ライフル銃の形をした連続写真撮影機である写真銃を発明した医学・生理学者エティエンヌ=ジュール・マレー（1830-1904）の影響を受け、連続写真をイメージし、直線や色彩の明暗、グラデーションを活かして絵画化した。   ⑨サイン 画面右下に「BALLA 1912」と黒で署名。   ⑩鑑賞のポイント 「走る馬は20本の脚を持つ」という1910年に発表された「未来派絵画技術宣言」の有名な記述を図示した作品。バッラは、光と運動の物理的現象をとらえようと、1912年5月にシエーナ県モンテプルチャーノで教え子のひとりであるネラッツィーニ伯爵夫人を訪ね、愉快なダックスフントと飼い主のバラバラとした足取りを描いた。ピンクと黄緑の横縞模様をした温かい背景は、明るい夏の太陽の下で輝くトスカーナの田園地帯の白い砂塵を表わしている。女性の足、鎖のリード、そして赤茶色の目をした犬［図1］の鼻先から尻尾［図2］まで、すべてが繰り返され、ぼかされている。スピード感を強調するため、バッラは背景の地面を斜線で描き、署名と日付も斜めの線に合わせて配置した。このリズミカルな表現は、額縁にもおよび、ステッチのような装飾が施されている。速度をユーモラスに視覚化したバッラの代表作であり、未来派を象徴する名作である。   図1 赤茶色した犬の目（《鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム》部分）   図2 9本描かれた尻尾（《鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム》部分）   スピードの違いを描き分ける 《鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム》について太田氏は、「ちょっとかわいい絵で、人によってはキッチュだと言うかもしれないが、実は一番実りの多い未来派20年の先駆け的な絵。本作と同年に制作された《バルコニーを走る少女》、また1913年から14年の「抽象的速度」シリーズにつながる速度や運動を表現した作品である。足元がクローズアップされていて面白い構図だ。画面全体はシンプルでモノクロームに見える。ただ足のこの回転というか、カカカッと動いている部分が、若桑先生が授業で説明していたように『天才バカボン』を描いた赤塚不二夫の漫画と言いたくなる。尻尾も回転し、女性の足も回転している。でも犬の方が回転が速く、犬と人のスピードの違いまで描き分けているのが凄い」と述べた。 また、太田氏は「未来派の絵画は、アメリカなど外国のコレクターに早い時期から人気があった。《鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム》は早くから注目されており、作品を買ったのは当時MoMAの初代理事長だったA・コンガー・グッドイヤーだ。MoMAでは、1936年に初代館長のアルフレッド・H・バー・Jr.が企画した「キュビスムと抽象芸術」展が開かれ、未来派の初期作品として《鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム》が展示された。バーの妻マーガレット・スコラーリの父はイタリア人で、美術史家だったマーガレットは1934年にローマのバッラを訪ねて、おそらく《鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム》を実見後、館長のバーが正式に手紙を送って展覧会の貸し出し交渉をしたと思われる。バッラは作品を売ってもいいと考えていたが、バーは丁重にお断りしたという。その時は売れなかったが、1938年に理事長のグッドイヤーが個人として購入した。その後MoMAには収蔵されず、1964年グッドイヤー家よりオルブライト=ノックス美術館（現バッファローAKG美術館）へ寄贈された」と作品の来歴について語った。   太田岳人（おおた・たけと） 千葉大学・東京科学大学・明治学院大学非常勤講師／イタリア近現代美術史研究者。1979年愛知県生まれ。2003年千葉大学文学部史学科卒業、2005年同大学大学院文学研究科人文科学専攻修士課程修了、2010年～2011年ローマ大学文学・哲学部留学、2013年千葉大学大学院社会文化科学研究科日本研究専攻博士課程修了。博士（文学）。専門：未来派を中心とするイタリア近現代美術史。所属学会：イタリア学会、美学会、日伊協会、イタリア言語・文化研究会、イタリア近現代史研究会。主な論文：「イタリア・ファシズム政権期の未来派 ——1930年代を中心に」（博士論文、千葉大学大学院社会文化科学研究科、2013）、「漫画作品から絵本へ：『ムナーリの機械』の制作過程に関する一考察」（『早稲田大学イタリア研究所研究紀要NO.9』早稲田大学地域・地域間研究機構 イタリア研究所研究紀要編集委員会、2020）、「〈未来派航空絵画宣言〉を読む : 1930 年代における包括的な芸術運動のためのテキスト」（『立命館言語文化研究 No.145』立命館大学国際言語文化研究所、2021）、「イタリア未来派の諸宣言の日本語訳」（『立命館言語文化研究Vol.34, No.3』立命館大学国際言語文化研究所、2023）、「日本におけるイタリア未来派受容——図像の伝播を中心に」（図録『イタリアと日本の前衛』水声社、2024）など。   ジャコモ・バッラ（Giacomo Balla） イタリアの画家、彫刻家。1871〜1958年。イタリア北西部ピエモンテ州の州都トリノ生まれ。1886年トリノの美術学校予科に通う。1891年学校を中退し、写真家オレステ・ベルティエーリのスタジオに職を得る。分割主義の画法を知り、同年「トリノ美術振興協会」の展覧会に初出品する。1892年頃トリノ大学でチェーザレ・ロンブローゾに師事。1895年母とローマに転居。1899年ヴェネツィア・ビエンナーレに出品。1900年パリに半年間滞在する。1902年未来派で後に同志となるセヴェリーニとボッチョーニに分割主義技法を教える。1904年エリーザ・マルクッチと結婚し、二人の娘をもうける。1909年イタリアの詩人マリネッティが「未来派創立宣言」発表。1910年には光・運動の研究を始め、「未来派画家宣言」「未来派絵画技術宣言」の共同署名者となる。1911年ローマの公的展覧会「イタリア統一50周年展」に参加。1912年《鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム》制作。抽象的な色彩研究を始める。1913年「抽象的速度」シリーズ開始。作風を刷新し、サインに「Futurballa」と署名するようになった。1914年「反中立服装宣言」を発表。1915年フォルトゥナート・デペロと「宇宙の未来派的再構築宣言」を共同で発表。1916年「未来派映画」の撮影に参加。1917年バレエ・リュスのローマ公演『花火』の舞台装置をデザイン。1918年応用芸術へ関心を示し、「色彩宣言」を発表。1921年ナイトクラブ「バル・ティク・タク」の内装を手掛ける。1931年具象への回帰が表われ、「未来派航空絵画宣言」の共同署名者となる。1935年ローマのサン・ルカ美術アカデミー会員になる。1937年「ペルセオ」紙への書簡で未来派と絶縁していると公表。1947年ニューヨーク近代美術館から作品購入の打診。1958年3月1日ローマにて死去。享年87歳。代表作：《鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム》《破産》《アーク灯》など。   デジタル画像のメタデータ タイトル：鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム。作者：影山幸一。主題：世界の絵画。内容記述：ジャコモ・バッラ《鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム》1912年、キャンバス・油彩、縦89.9×横109.9cm、米国ニューヨーク州、バッファローAKG美術館蔵。公開者：（株）DNPアートコミュニケーションズ。寄与者：バッファローAKG美術館、Bridgeman Images、（株）DNPアートコミュニケーションズ。日付：─。資源タイプ：イメージ。フォーマット：Jpeg形式51.0MB、300dpi、8bit、RGB。資源識別子：BAL_53112（Jpeg形式52.4MB、300dpi、8bit、RGB、カラーガイド・グレースケールなし）。情報源：（株）DNPアートコミュニケーションズ。言語：日本語。体系時間的・空間的範囲：─。権利関係：バッファローAKG美術館、Bridgeman Images、（株）DNPアートコミュニケーションズ。   画像製作レポート 《鎖に繋がれた犬のダイナミズム》の画像は、DNPアートコミュニケーションズ（DNPAC）へメールで依頼した。後日、DNPACからのメールにより、作品画像をダウンロードして入手（Jpeg、52.4MB、300dpi、8bit、RGB、カラーガイド・グレースケールなし）。トリミング2点、掲載は1年間。 iMac 21インチモニターをEye-One Display2（X-Rite）によって、モニターを調整する。バッファローAKG美術館のホームページ上の作品の画像を参考に色調整をし、枠に沿って切り抜いた（Jpeg形式51.0MB、300dpi、8bit、RGB）。バッラが額装も制作した作品なので、額付きの画像を探したが入手ができず残念だった。また、1958年に死亡したバッラの日本での著作権は、死亡年から50年経過した2008年に消滅していた。日本美術著作権協会によると「日本の著作権の保護期間は、2018年12月30日の法改正によって70年に延長されているが、すでに消滅した作家の権利はよみがえることがない。第二次世界大戦での戦勝国である連合国（米国、英国、フランスなど）の国籍を有する作家には、戦時中に著作権が保護されなかったことへの敗戦国、わが国に課された代償として敗戦国には約10年の戦時加算が付与されており、1958年に死亡した連合国国籍の作家には保護の対象になる作品も存在する。この作家はイタリア国籍のため、それには該当しない」とのことであった。 Editore, 2000） ・井関正昭『未来派 イタリア・ロシア・日本』（形文社、2003.6.6） ・Fabio Benzi, Giacomo Balla: genio futurista（Electa, 2007） ・Giovanni Lista, Balla: La modernità futurista（Skira, 2008） items.body: Some records ask to be heard; Philippe Petit’s Lightning Field 01. Constraint asks to be observed, documenting the unpredictable conversation between composer, electricity, and machine at the heart of modular synthesis. Fragments of a larger ongoing investigation Modulisme Session 144. Lightning Field 01. Constraint by Philippe Petit   Modular synthesis releases occupy a deeply specific and persistently misunderstood territory within experimental electronic music—a territory that operates by entirely different rules than those governing conventional recorded sound. These aren’t listening experiences in the expected sense. They’re dispatches. Evidence gathered from the interior of a process most listeners will never witness directly. A conversation conducted between a composer and a system that has its own grammar, its own tolerance for deviation, its own appetite for accident. The best of them carry no trace of manufacture. They feel discovered rather than designed, unearthed from the space between human decision and machine response. At its most essential, the modular release functions less like composition and more like field recording, the distinction being that the field here is electrical, the landscape assembled from patch cables, voltage gradients, and the irreducible uncertainty that lives in the gap between what a composer instructs and what a system chooses to return. Modulisme—the platform born in July 2019 out of Marseille, described as a media documenting left-field modular synthesis, has been building this archive since its inception, reaching session 144 here. The platform operates like a library rather than a label, curating exclusive one-hour sessions from composers working with modular systems across the full range of the form, from academic electroacoustic tradition through to experimental improvisation and everything in between. By session 144, the catalog represents over a thousand exclusive works and a genuine document of where modular synthesis composition stands in the mid-2020s. The artist behind Modulisme is Philippe Petit himself—a Marseille-born composer, DJ, label operator, and self-described “musical travel agent” who has been releasing work since 2000 across labels including Sub Rosa, Monotype, Home Normal, Staubgold, and his own BiP_HOp imprint, which from 2000 to 2010 advocated left-field electronica before eventually becoming Modulisme. He studied electroacoustic music at the CNRR Conservatory, specializing in multi-channeled diffusion and modular synthesis, working with Buchla System 200, Serge 73/75, and a modified EMS Synthi A. His catalog includes collaborations with Lydia Lunch, Edward Ka-Spel, Eugene S. Robinson, and a genuinely vast network of experimental musicians accumulated over decades of restless cross-genre activity. He describes himself not as a composer but as someone who transmigrates source material, an apt description for an artist whose work has always been about the movement between forms rather than the forms themselves. Electricity itself as the subject rather than a medium :: Lightning Field 01. Constraint is the first volume of a new series in which Petit imposes a specific limitation on himself: no acoustic instruments, no vocals, no field recordings. The usual escape routes he describes reaching for in composition—a piano frame, a prepared guitar, voices, found sounds, are deliberately removed. What remains is his Buchla and Serge systems working in isolation, and the results of letting those systems define the boundaries of what’s possible. The title is precise, this is a volume about the founding decision, the acceptance of voluntary limitation, and what that limitation reveals. It’s the same constraint logic that has driven the most interesting experimental music for decades, from Alvin Lucier‘s single-premise compositions to the Oulipo literary movement’s rule-based writing. What happens when you remove the familiar? What surfaces in the space left behind? What surfaces here is a series of works that treat electricity itself as the subject rather than a medium. Petit describes the modular as a miniature weather system whose internal architecture has been laid bare, not an instrument but a machine for intimate storms. That’s not marketing language. It’s an accurate description of how Buchla and Serge systems behave in the hands of someone who understands their particular logic. Unlike Eurorack, which tends toward precision and control, the Buchla and Serge traditions lean toward instability, drift, and the productive unpredictability of analog voltage. A patch on a Buchla system creates relationships between modules that interact and evolve in ways that can’t be fully predicted in advance. The composer sets conditions rather than issuing instructions. What emerges from those conditions is the work. The tracks themselves are labeled in iterations: “Field 04,” “Field 05,” “Field 06,” and so on, through to “Field 15.” Each one is a short burst of electronic bubbles and modular clicks, some containing feedback, others carrying rhythm. They function less as tracks in the conventional sense and more as specimens, individual electrical events captured and named sequentially rather than titled descriptively. That naming convention is itself a statement about what these pieces are. They’re not songs. They’re not compositions in the way that word is usually understood. They’re fragments of a larger ongoing investigation, numbered because they occurred in an order, not because they need to be experienced in one. This recalls the classic modular sessions of the 1970s and 80s, the early Moog explorations of Wendy Carlos, whose Switched-On Bach (1968) introduced the synthesizer to mainstream audiences but whose later works like Sonic Seasonings (1972) pushed into more abstract, atmospheric territory. Klaus Schulze‘s extended Berlin School synthesizer pieces, Tangerine Dream‘s Phaedra and Rubycon, Morton Subotnick‘s Silver Apples of the Moon (1967)—the first electronic work commissioned by a record label, and the musique concrète lineage running through Pierre Henry and Bernard Parmegiani at INA/GRM in Paris all share the same fundamental question Petit is asking here: what does electricity sound like when you stop trying to make it sound like something else? The longest track in the batch is “Field 06,” running at 11:08, and it’s the most melodic of the bunch. It opens with a sequence arp cycling through different tones, rhythms going off-tone and on again, speeds shifting, different oscillators being introduced and withdrawn. More than any other piece here it plays on the melodic and rhythmic side of modular synthesis—the arp becoming a kind of unstable melody, never quite resolving, always pointing somewhere it doesn’t arrive. Much of what’s played throughout the series sits in distortions and rhythms rather than conventional melodic structure, which is consistent with Petit‘s stated intention to let the systems generate the conditions rather than imposing a compositional outcome on top of them. This is not for the casual listener. That needs to be stated plainly. You won’t find structural familiarity here, no verse-chorus logic, no emotional arc that announces itself. These are pieces, not tracks, electrical specimens, experiments in what a Buchla and Serge system will produce when given a set of conditions and allowed to follow its own logic. This is Session 144, and the fact that it’s Petit‘s own session rather than a guest is significant. He built this platform to document the modular synthesis community and has spent years giving that platform to others. Turning the session on himself, and specifically doing so under a constraint he describes as deliberate, as a way of denying himself the usual escape routes, suggests this isn’t a casual exercise. Lightning Field is announced as a series, meaning this first volume of constraint is the beginning of something longer and more sustained. Not obsessively themed, but genuinely exploratory, each volume investigating the same territory from a different angle, the synthesizer as an active field through which forces circulate rather than a machine that produces predetermined outcomes. For an artist who has spent over two decades documenting what other people do with electricity and cables and voltage, this is Petit finally turning the recording equipment on himself and letting his own storm be captured. The sound is no longer manufactured. It is, as he writes, captured. Guided. Transmuted. Whether that transmutation continues to reveal new territory across future Lightning Field volumes is the question worth watching. Session 144 makes a compelling case that it will. items.body: The finest quality of Ladybug 1 comes from its ability to treat dub as an art of emotional memory. Each return of the theme seems to erase something and make it more vivid at the same time. In the leaner versions, rhythm becomes a heavy step through smoke, reverbs widen like liquid metal, silences speak with the same intensity as the impacts. Vanishing is the core and the fate of the whole EP Ladybug 1 by The Bug / Dis Fig   With Ladybug 1 EP, Kevin Richard Martin opens the Ladybug series on Pressure through a work of emotional precision. Each chapter will bring a different female voice into his bass universe, and the first presence is Dis Fig, Felicia Chen, already a crucial companion on In Blue (Hyperdub). The memory of that album returns like a call from the dark, and here the step shifts, the air grows warmer, the pulse slows, the matter turns more bodily. The Bug has shaped, across decades, a language immediately his own, born from dub, dancehall, industrial music, spectral hip hop, sound system devotion and lab fever. Chen comes from another fire, formed through noise culture, club practice, wounded vocality and physical performance. Together they find a zone where song becomes atmospheric pressure, and dub moves from genre into inner weather. Vanishing is the core and the fate of the whole EP. Around the main piece, versions, dubs and deeper immersions expand the same emotional event, as Martin opens the body of the music and reveals nerves, vapor, rhythmic apparatus, magnetic blood. The choice moves beyond the simple idea of a remix set and takes on an almost cinematic form: one ghost seen from different angles, one trauma changing density at every pass. The bass carries the weight of a horizon drawing near, pushing from below, bending the light. The percussion advances slowly, with the authority of a machine that knows the measure of pain. Around it, ambient trails, dub vapors, shoegaze reflections and exhausted sensuality gather into music that feels vast, physical, tender in its devastation. It is dub for the end of love, soul for immense systems, electronics speaking to the body before thought. A series debut with the force of something necessary: a handful of tracks, a single emotional center, a depth that grows with every listen. ~Mirco Salvadori Dis Fig’s singing is the point where this mass receives a face. Her voice descends along the lines of sound, melts into the kick, then rises again like a private confession caught by an apparatus far too powerful. The lyrics, written by Chen, seem to follow disappearance after a romantic rupture: the loss of the loved body, the numbness after impact, desire continuing to send signals after contact has faded. The word Vanishing becomes gesture, phenomenon, progressive erasure, almost a way of naming the fading of the self inside the echo of another. Chen sings with feverish grace, close to secular prayer and stripped soul, letting fragility, narcotic sweetness, muted resentment and burning lucidity pass through. Her presence turns the brutality of the low end into feeling, gives the machine a human breath, carries the wound to the center of the system. The finest quality of Ladybug 1 comes from its ability to treat dub as an art of emotional memory. Each return of the theme seems to erase something and make it more vivid at the same time. In the leaner versions, rhythm becomes a heavy step through smoke, reverbs widen like liquid metal, silences speak with the same intensity as the impacts. Martin’s hand knows the tradition of the mixing desk as creative instrument, the lesson of Scientist, the daring of On U Sound, the hypnotic depth of Basic Channel, the mutant melancholy of King Midas Sound. Here those lines enter a new tale, more feverish and sentimental, where sound system culture meets a broken ballad, lover’s rock is projected into a digital night, and Massive Attack appears as a distant memory filtered through exhausted subwoofers. Ladybug 1 chooses concentration. Each impact carries weight, each halo has narrative function, each sonic ghost guides listening toward a feeling of separation that becomes a mental landscape. ~Mirco Salvadori The strength of the brief format lies in its visionary economy. Five passages, a single title changing skin, a progression shaped through subtraction and fever, with the sound seeming to grow larger as ornament falls away. Martin sculpts low air with the patience of a craftsman and the fury of an engineer of controlled collapse; Chen cuts a melodic line across the surface of the magma, curving, trembling, touching silence, then rising again with an almost soul like grace. In a moment when much contemporary music confuses intensity with accumulation, Ladybug 1 chooses concentration. Each impact carries weight, each halo has narrative function, each sonic ghost guides listening toward a feeling of separation that becomes a mental landscape. Ladybug 1 therefore works as a miniature manifesto. It introduces a future series and says plenty about the present of The Bug: the urgency to keep collaborating, to offer his architecture of pressure to voices able to carry risk, desire and biography. For Dis Fig, this return feels like another change of state: from the floating presence of In Blue to a dominant emotional figure, able to bend Martin’s matter toward an abstract blues for saturated times. The music moves slowly, sensually, menacingly, with a beauty born from compression more than explosion. It is dub for the end of love, soul for immense systems, electronics speaking to the body before thought. A series debut with the force of something necessary: a handful of tracks, a single emotional center, a depth that grows with every listen. Ladybug 1 is available on Pressure. items.body: “Qué Loquera”, roughly “What Madness”, is a merengue-driven satire of a planet cooking itself, and of the lovesick singer going down with it. As the world falls apart, Nene del Solar reaches for aguapacheo, his word for wet-kissing on the dancefloor, as the way to carry the grief of man-made catastrophe. The song runs deconstructed Caribbean rhythms, digital synthesisers and chanted onomatopoeia into salsa tumbaos rewired for the dancefloor. It takes the dance straight through the madness of its title, and its AI-generated video turns the tool on itself, a direct hit at artificial intelligence, tech-bros and the way digital life burns through the planet, made by Fabián Mosele and Ali Bardavid. That mix of homemade tropical machines and end-of-the-world dread puts the track in the frame of Caribbean futurism: speculative art that faces down climate collapse and the plunder of the Global South from the region’s own rhythms and beliefs, keeping the machines and dropping the worship of them. The single opens Donde Hay Calor, the debut album from Nene del Solar, released on 17 July through In-Correcto, the Bogotá collective and label that has spent a decade gathering the city’s cumbia, rap, folk and electronic outliers.   Behind the alias is Icaro Lopez de Mesa Moyano, a Colombian sound-media artist who builds the motorised percussion he plays and calls it Los Robots del Ritmo. He works between Bogotá and Bremen, where he is a doctoral candidate, with eight years of traditional Latin American music training behind him, an industrial design degree from Colombia’s National University and a digital media masters from Germany. His projects have played Rock Al Parque at home and SXSW in Texas. Stream “Qué Loquera” HERE and pick up your copy of Donde Hay Calor following THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Nene del Solar – Qué Loquera appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by alainPP — 1. "Can I Tell You" is the opening track from this unique violin-led band?a gritty, rhythmic rock number sitting somewhere between classic and symphonic rock; a fresh experience delivering explosive rock energy.2. "Bringing It Back" kicks off with boogie-woogie piano; the violin and Robbie's vocals drive an energetic, swirling groove. A new sound is born here?one that's hard to pin down to specific influences because it feels entirely original.3. "Lonely Wind" features piano and vocals, with Steve sharing lead duties; note Phil's delicate touch and Kerry's warm keyboards on this killer slow ballad.4. "Belexes" arrives with high-energy keyboards engaging in a musical duel. The melody flows like glowing embers tumbling down a slope; the organ is on fire?fittingly so?and the backing vocals are in full swing. Rich, sporting his signature headband, delivers a sharp, high-pitched guitar solo, cementing the band's trademark blend of keyboards, guitar, and violin. The track heats up further with a final drum solo that sets the listener's ears ablaze.5. "Journey From Mariabronn" is the first of three epic-length tracks; with its violin variations and piano melody, I detect a nod to Supertramp. The song bears a progressive stamp reminiscent of Queen, while the keyboards evoke Yes?heavy stuff! Dave's bass anchors everything and drives the momentum; in short, a magnificent piece of prog rock.6. "The Pilgrimage" returns to a blend of pop, rock, folk, and boogie with a touch of Southern rock flair?thanks to the violin and backing vocals?though it's a bit too brief to truly hook the listener.7. "Apercu" offers a more substantial experience, opening with a spirited energy that leads into verses shared by the two frontmen. The violin ushers in an instrumental section with clear folk undertones, infusing the music with a festive spirit?a fantastic glimpse into their fusion of rock and symphonic styles. The finale takes on an elegiac tone, introduced by a solemn violin before shifting into heavy?or rather hard?rock, driven by the sheer power of the drums and guitar; this intensity carries over into the next track:8. "Death Of Mother Nature Suite," a true grand finale for this distinctive debut album. Here, heavy rock weightiness blends with a melancholic violin. The song navigates shifting harmonic textures, balancing tender sensitivity with the fiery power of the chorus?where the backing vocals truly shine. The guitar solo serves as an immediate reminder that Kansas is a band of the highest caliber. It was undoubtedly a stunning achievement for the genre of folk-infused heavy rock.

items.body: Review by Circuito_Prog — With Pestkr�nikene, Jordsj� celebrates its tenth anniversary without relying on easy nostalgia. Even though the album is built from material written between 2020 and 2025, the Norwegian duo gives it a strong identity and a cohesive concept centered on war, the fall of ancient kingdoms, religious fanaticism, and rebuilding after devastation. Rather than feeling like a collection of leftovers, it stands as one of the band's most cohesive releases.Musically, Jordsj� reinforces the sound that has made them one of the leading names in modern Scandinavian progressive rock. The analog warmth of the production, the prominent use of flute, vintage keyboards, and the balance between pastoral passages and heavier moments create a distinctly Nordic atmosphere. You'll hear echoes of Jethro Tull, Wobbler, �nglag�rd, and even touches of Gentle Giant or Anekdoten, but the band never loses its own identity.One of the album's greatest strengths is how much it accomplishes in just 35 minutes. In a genre often dominated by sprawling epics, Jordsj� opts for compact compositions, most of them between three and five minutes long, keeping the album moving at a steady pace without ever feeling overstuffed. That brevity occasionally makes a few ideas seem to end a little too soon, but it also makes Pestkr�nikene an engaging listen that rewards repeated plays with its intricate details.The guest appearances by Jon A. Henriksen, Andreas Prestmo, and Lars Fredrik Fr�islie add plenty of depth without overshadowing the creative partnership of H�kon Oftung and Kristian Fr�land. Each musician brings something unique to the record, while the production maintains the organic, handcrafted feel that sets it apart from many contemporary releases.Pestkr�nikene doesn't reinvent progressive rock, but it proves there's still plenty of room to expand its boundaries while staying rooted in tradition. It's an album filled with rich atmospheres, memorable melodies, and carefully crafted arrangements that further establishes Jordsj� as one of the most consistent bands in today's European progressive rock scene. It may not reach the grand scale of some of the genre's biggest landmarks, but its authenticity, balance, and genuine love for classic progressive rock make it one of the most worthwhile releases of 2026. items.body: Review by alainPP — Hawkestrel is Alan Davey releasing this 17th opus, distilling the energy of his diverse body of work. Tracks spanning space rock, prog, psych, jazz, and metal, featuring guest artists and original band members. A collection of sensational Hawkwind covers alongside reworkings of songs by Led Zeppelin, the Beach Boys, and Cream."Hall of the Mountain Grill"?featuring piano and flute?is a 1974 track where I find myself desperately searching for Grieg's influence. It is a dark cover, enhanced by Simon's brooding violin. "Brainstorm" channels a Murkey Red vibe?a wild, stoner-punk-psych hybrid blending thick synth, violin, and sax into an apoplectic maelstrom. "Rainbow Demon," an Uriah Heep cover, delivers the organ and riffs of an era before "hard rock" even had a name; Mick's shimmering guitar evokes a vintage feel that invites a nostalgic trip back in time. "Sunshine of Your Love" resurrects Cream's raw, unadorned sound?Ginger's drumming and that vibrant riff flirting with gritty, snarling rock. "Children of the Sun" transports us back to 1971; a heavy riff meets fiery violin, creating a driving track that surfs on psychedelic clouds. Del lets his synth spiral wildly?a touch of Hawkwind meets Ozric Tentacles. "Subterraneans" features vocals reminiscent of Bowie's Robert-era style and a reverberating atmosphere?proto-space-rock "fudge" ahead of its time. Notes swirl, soaking the track in the nascent vibe of early space rock; it ends with an airplane-style outro."Black Dog" features female vocals and Keith's keyboards bursting joyfully out of the solar system?a rhythmic psychedelic cover. "Starcruiser" stands out for its intro?just the way I like it?with Michael's distinctive voice driving a frenetic psych-rock track filled with swirling, wind-like synth sounds. "The Greenfly and The Rose" sees Michael continuing the set, accompanied by a medieval-sounding organ. The drift continues?a pre-emptive stutter of cold wave, pompous art-rock, and Southern rock?floating through cottony limbo. "The Cairene Purse" unfolds over a *Flash Gordon*-esque synth line, a narrative interlude transporting the listener elsewhere to explore a story born of the artist's imagination. "Good Vibrations" is revisited through a psychedelic lens, evoking the latent atmosphere of a parallel universe?as if the Beach Boys had truly conceived the track as a prog-psych-rock testament in the vein of Hawkwind.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A Dutch blues-rock jam band who aspired to Kosmische-style jazz-rock music and, in fact, notably were successful at creating their own particular kind of jazz-rock music while coming from Traffic- and The Who-like blues-rock perspectives.1. "Saras Ritt Durch Schwarzwald" (6:23) impressive Who-like Rock approaching Hawkwind-like Prog or Krautrock. I love Johannes Pappert's Arabian/Indian-styled sax play in the fourth and fifth minute's "interlude." The singing (in Dutch) is like a cross between CAN and early Ozzie. (8.75/10)2. "M.C. Escher" (6:14) the organ-base to the first minute of this one makes it feel like URIAH HEEP but then Johannes' sax enters, taking the wind out of the heavy rock vibe. At the end of the second minute the music totally changes (though still using the same instrumental palette): driving rock drums and bass with long-sustained organ chords. A reliance on a set "heavy metal" guitar chord progression is also reminiscent of bands like Heep, Sabbath, Deep Purple, and Nektar. A brief "normal" voiced lyric in the middle is interesting for its educational attempt. (8.6667/10)3. "Kraan Arabia" (9:45) another droning near-"heavy metal" song that is so quintessentially Krautrock is most notable for the way it exploits Johannes' Arabian sounding and melodic sensibilities on his saxophone. There are a couple sound effects switches on the sax and a few windows for Peter Wolbrandt's rhythm guitar and lead guitar to step into the spotlight. And, damn! Hellmut Hattler is a solid and yet fluid bass player. Note the flange effect placed upon the mics recording Jan Fride's cymbals. The laughter and "smoke-break" breakdown in the eighth minute is rather FOCUS- and CAN-like but it also enables Hellmut the chance to solo a bit (not as good of a soloist as rhythmatist) as well as Jan to show off his conga and supplemental percussion instrumental skills while also showcasing more of Peter's guitar skills (also a great rhythmatist). (17.75/20)4. "Head" (18:36) impressive display of rhythmic expression and group unity--especially from Hellmut and Jan. Too bad about the somewhat cheesy riffs borrowed from British rockers like The Who. (35.5/40)5. "Sara auf der Gansewies" (2:01) bluesy cinema music using sax and guitar doubled up to present the plaintive main melody and bass. I like it though it is nothing Earth-shatteringly innovative. (4.375/5)Total Time: 42:59A rock album that draws from a lot of diverse influences including a Krautrock foundation that is heavily steeped in Can-like Kosmische Musik, Steve Winwood organ-based Blues-Rock, The Who's new and more concise Rock 'n' Roll, Chicago Transit Authority jazz-rock, and many of the psychedelic influences that tap into (or arise from) Middle Eastern and Oriental influences. It is also obvious that the band had heard Can, King Crimson, Brainbox/Focus, The Who, and The Mahavishnu Orchestra. Despite their jazzification of a lot of their instrumental performances, the music here feels quite solidly founded in blues-rock structures and motifs--which makes them feel much more akin to bands like The Spencer Davis Group and Traffic. They may have been inspired by The Mahavishnu Orchestra but they sound to me much more like Ash Ra Tempel, Amon D��l II, and/or Can. And, yes: Hellmut Hattler is a GREAT bass player! (How 'bout bringing he and Can's Jaki Liebezeit together with Triumvirat's J�rgen Fritz and Jan Akkerman for a Teutonic super super-group!)B-/3.5 stars; a nice addition to any prog rocker's music collection--especially if s/he is interested in the early foundational music of Krautrock, European Heavy Metal, and/or psychedelic prog.

"Zion I" (3:27) despite the Afro-Jamaican roots being expressed here, there is a laid-back sophistication here that predicts the direction that the band WAR would be taking in a couple years. (8.875/10)A2. "One More" (3:04) more laid back Afro-Caribbean sounds that incorporate bagpipe-like sounding instrument into the mix (as a kind of background reinforcer of the main guitar melody during the "choruses"). Satisfying if not fully developed: more like a little warm-up jam or �tude. (8.75/10)A3. "Getting It Back" (4:17) a bit of the drama of The Undisputed Truth and Nina Simone present in both the music and vocal performance. The horns are little too unified, harmonized too synchronically, even though the sax gets to break free and solo a bit in the final minute. (8.6667/10)A4. "Listen" (4:39) another song whose foundation sounds like it's informed by the current trends in American Soul/R&B being by Stax and Motown bands like Ike & Tina Turner, The Staples Singers, and the new kids on the block, The Undisputed Truth. A little boring with its endlessly repeating bass and melody lines. (8.6667/10)A5. "Rickshaw" (5:53) a motif that feels as if it carries over some of the worldly amalgamations achieved at the end of the 1960s by film soundtrack composers like Henry Mancini (Blake Edwards films), Burt Bacharach, and even Eric Burdon's War ("Spill the Wine"). (8.875/10)B1. "Dove" (10:52) a psychedelic jazz-blues jam that sounds like it came straight from San Francisco (Love, Santana, even a little of The Doors) Really nice, satisfying SANTANA-like jam with great groove and lead guitar work from Patrick Patterson. (18.25/20)B2. "Bra" (5:03) more Stax Studios-like Soul/R&B music with a catchy lyric sung in choral chant style. Great bass, drums, rhythm guitar groove with perfect brass section arrangements. (9.125/10)B3. "The Message" (4:19) one of the band's more popular tunes--both as an anthem and as a concert crowd-pleaser. It's a little simple and rather monotonous but apparently the words have significance that draw people in. (8.75/10)B4. "Rastafarian Folk Song" (3:09) exhibiting as fact that not all Jamaican or Rastafarian music is or has to be registered/rendered as Reggae music. Well presented as both engaging music as well as educational fodder. (8.875/10)Total Time 44:43What I hear here is a band who feels that it is their mission to unify African and Caribbean musical traditions with the Soul and Rhythm & Blues of the United States--to open the minds of Anglo-Americans to the interracial trends toward blending and fusion that had been emerging with the 1960s Civil Rights Movement and Anti-War, anti-establishment, counter-cultural revolution.B/four stars; a nice collection of fairly simple Afro-Caribbean Soul/R&B that has two highlight songs. I'd consider this more proto-prog than straightforward prog, Jazz-Rock, or J-R Fusion.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the more unusual progressive bands to emerge from the 1970s boom in the Netherlands, HETPANDORRA ENSEMBLE existed from 1973 until 1980 and left one album in its wake and very little infoabout its existence with nobody even sure of where the band was formed exactly. This band that wasled by guitarist Dolf Planteijdt who eschewed the symphonic prog tendencies of fellow Dutch actslike Focus or even more pop-fueled vocal acts like Earth & Fire but rather the band featured abizarre mishmash of heavy King Crimson guitar angst, Mahavishnu Orchestra inspired jazz fusion andextreme free improvisation liberties with varying musical motifs suddenly shifting midstream intosomething completely different. In addition to the more contemporary prog references, this band wasalso smitten with the abstract modern classical styles of George Crumb as well as impressionistssuch as Ravel and Bartok's Eastern European folklore works.The ENSEMBLE's entire presentation itself was a little odd with this act featuring only five membersand releasing a single album ironically titled III in 1978. What makes it even weirder is that thecover looks like a Patti Smith reject which honestly conveys absolutely nothing about the musicinside. No wonder this talented band was overlooked and lost to the annals of time! The lineup onIII features the cast members of Planteijdt (guitars), Dolf Planteijdt (guitars), Roland Brunt(flute), Gert-Jan Blom (bass) and Wilfred Snellens who replaced the recently deceased Jean Eble. Thealbum was released on the Disaster Electronics label and originally featured five tracks however the2012 Modulus reissue adds an extra seven bonus tracks of unreleased material.For all its eclecticism, HET PANDORRA ENSEMBLE was primarily steeped in complex jazz fusion motifsthat incorporated angular avant-prog complexities and King Crimson's "Red" as a template for gnarledguitar tones. The album displays a fairly interesting balance between skronky dissonance and morecleverly constructed melodic touches implementing everything from moments of space rock to Spanishflamenco. Three tracks "Door Mekaar," "Kanon Pittoresk" and "Karotten" all extend past the 10-minuteplaying time while the remaining two are much shorter clocking in under 5. "Kanon Pittoresk" is theperfect example of this band's extremities meandering from super chill to ridiculously sped uptempos and sizzling guitar soloing with a rather Latin-inspired bass groove. The band's album iscompletely instrumental with no vocals except a very a single moment of wordless chanting."Door Mekaar" showcases a reimagined King Crimson take on jazz fusion with twin guitar attacks andover-the-top complex arrangements while "Kanon Pittoresk" is more of a wild free-for-all that deftlyblends angular avant-prog fusion with more melodic rock hybridizations. The short track "Ritme 7000"serves only as a palette cleanser. It has sort of a medieval folk feel but only distantly. "Drei"takes a complete 180 and introduces a chamber rock style with a lengthy shrill monotone that slowlygenerates a creepy mood setting that pretty much stays in droning mode for 4 1/2 minutes with only afew surprise vocal chants and occasional tinkling of random sounds. "Karotten" ends the album withcontinues the detached eeriness of its predecessor and slowly transmogrifies into a guitar drivenseries of KC inspired works that evolve into a more fiery example of jazz fusion thus taking thealbum full circle. HET PANDORRA ENSEMBLE was sort of the fish out of water and even though it joined the ranks of theprog universe late in the game still retained that fiery experimental passion that exploded in thelate 1960s and became somewhat commercialized by 1973. III is a rather unpredictable slice of Dutchprog that sounds like no other. A second album was in the works but never came to fruition leaving aslew of musical carcasses to gather dust on the shelves for many decades before finally emerging asa whopping double album reissue in 2012. While the album could use some fine-tuning to make it morecohesive and sometimes feels extremely disjointed, for those with an appetite for wild untamedartistry run amok then this one will prove quite satisfying.

items.body: Review by Heart of the Matter — This fantastic concert, advertised as the "solo albums tour" in order to capitalize the expectatives originated in their 1975 sabatical, dedicated by each band member to their own project, remained until its 50th anniversary as a legendary, sought-after bootleg. Now officially released, it presents us with a Yes formation, including Patrick Moraz on keyboards (Wakeman's replacement), shining in the full splendour of their mid-seventies. Bold, exploratory and going full throttle from the start, the band is up to the energy level displayed in their previous studio release, the album Relayer. This is well represented here, of course, by Sound Chaser and the side-long epic The Gates of Delirium. Also, the same virtuosism and powerful sonic brilliance are put into the staple versions, such as Siberian Kathru and I've Seen All Good People, and an extraordinary rendition of Ritual, sending sparks from the bottom of those Topographic Oceans.The songs coming from the solo albums, in the form of excerpts taken from Jon Anderson's Olias Of Sunhillow and Moraz' Story Of I, offer a welcome relaxing moment, including also a newly fashioned, acoustic rendition of Long Distance Runaround, so brief as full of charm.What else? Oh, yeah, all this comes from the hearts and hands of musicians listening to each other tight, instead of to a metronome. Better to seize than to miss, don't you think?

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A second studio album put together in 1971 in London under the supervision of producer Tony Visconti (and also receiving the artistic talents of Roger Dean for the album art).1. "Beautiful Seven" (6:45) some soulful High Life music that has the advantage of Western rock production values to bring about better definition to and performances from each of the individual instruments. (Tony is figuring out how to mic and engineer this band!) The melodies, engineering, and mixes here are so much more superior to anything on the band's previous album (which was released within the same calendar year). The SANTANA-like jam that emerges in the final minute is what I've been looking more for. Still, the overall quality of the sound and performances is so much better than Osibisa. (13.75/15)2. "Y Sharp" (6:21) Memphis Blues-Rock sounding like it's coming straight out of the Stax recording studios--as if Isaac Hayes and David Porter were composing their music! Very enjoyable, nicely-polished mostly-instrumental music of a generic type that the musicians are embellishing with satisfactory spirit and inspiration. (9.125/10) 3. "Spirits Up Above" (7:18) a song that opens up sounding like PROCOL HARUM or THE SPENCER DAVIS GROUP setting up a ballad. But then the unusual tandem of trumpet and flute present the dirge-like melody lines over wah-wah-ed electric guitar and baritone sax. Wow! This is then trumped by the entrance and vocal presence of a church-like "Baptist" choir singing what could be a eulogy for a minute or so. Then the band suddenly kicks into Blues-Rock third gear with a two-chord vamp over which Robert Bailey's electric piano solos over Roy Bedeau and Sol Amarfino's excellent bass and drumming, respectively. Wendel Richardson's guitar solo is next and it's really cool with chord sliding and multi-note picking, all the while the horn section is supporting with its smooth long notes--until the seventh minute when the individual horns start to meander off onto their paths. What an awesome jam! This is by far the best thing I've heard from this band so far! (14.75/15)4. "Survival" (6:19) opening with some in-studio banter before Wendel (at least, I'm assuming it's Wendell) leading the band into a West African drum-and-chant opening (lasting 90 seconds!). I love this! And then at 1:45 the full band joins in, transitioning the music into some Memphis-ized High Life music--one that has some serious funk groovin' coming from Roy and Wendell as well as Robert's full organ chords and the tight horn section's accents and dominating lead melody blasts. In the middle of the fifth minute as Loughty Amao breaks free to solo with his tenor sax the rest of the band breaks into What's Going On-like party mingling noise in the background. Another awesome song! (9.5/10)5. "Move On" (4:34) opening with the "Oh-See-Bee-Sah" chant, the bass and percussion soon jump in with Wendel strumming acoustic guitar in a Django fashion to create a Caribbean-sounding High Life motif over which Wendel sings in a forceful Eric Burdon or Terry Kath-like singing voice and style, which changes the feel of the music into something more akin to War-like Jazz-Rock. Interesting. I like the sound palette, stylistic variety, but overall something's not quite working (besides the slightly murky overall mix). Maybe it's a bit over-filled: too busy; the Rock elements feel a little under-prepared and forced. (8.75/10)6. "Rabiatu" (5:07) a nice African-familiar High Life motif is taken into bluesier territory by all of the electrified instruments: Hammond organ, electric guitar, and watered-down bass line. The percussion line interlude in the third minute is cool--especially with Wendel's percussive rhythm guitar muted strumming and the deep, distant bass lines coming from both Ray's bass and Robert's Hammond. The horn work is very effective--very adeptly arranged. (8.875/10)7. "Woyaya" (4:27) PROCOL HARUM-like Hammond organ chords open this one before Wendel (barely) joins in to start the vocal choir up with his single-voiced recitation of the main lyric and melody, which is thereafter picked up by the whole band as a choir. They sound a bit like they're ending their night in an Irish pub with a drunken sing-a-long of some national (or local) anthem. Once they reach the fourth minute, as the choir join in singing the song title work over and over, things feel quite tight, but then they break into a percussion-only jam to finish it off for the final 45 seconds. Too bad! That "Woyaya" chant could've gone on a bit longer. A cool song--that could very easily be made into a whole-crowd anthem--that feels, to my mind, to be too loosely thrown together and condensed almost unnaturally when it could've been a nice eight or nine minute song. (8.875/10)Total Time: 40:44What a great leap forward for this band! Tony Visconti has figured the band out (proving his genius) and gotten superior sound, spirited performances of inspired compositions from this talented ensemble.A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of mostly very-well-produced, very well composed African Jazz Rock. Very highly recommended.
